Introduction


I. HISTORICAL BACKGROUNDS


The book of Micah plays a pivotal role in shaping the prophetic evaluation of the eighth century as a crucial time in the religious life of Judah and Israel. Nevertheless, the book’s content also reflects editorial activity from later eras.1 First, Micah’s early core of prophetic material deals with events in the latter part of the eighth century BCE. The second phase of the development of the book of Micah likely occurred in the aftermath of Jerusalem’s destruction, long after the lifetime of the eighth-century prophet for whom the book is named. This phase sought to clarify who was to blame for the events of 587. In this phase, editors incorporated chapters 6–7, creating an expansive update over the course of the sixth–fifth centuries BCE. The updates both affix blame for the destruction of Jerusalem in 587 BCE (6:1–7:7) and offer a salvific ending to the book (7:8–20). Finally, a later anthology (chapters 4–5) incorporates hopeful eschatological perspectives regarding the fate of Jerusalem and the nations while addressing the postexilic community. Because the final form of Micah takes shape over such a long time, a summary of the history of Judah and Israel over this time period will provide context for understanding the book as it came to be.





A. THE EIGHTH-CENTURY BACKGROUND OF THE EARLY CORE


Micah served as a prophet in the latter part of the eighth century BCE, and chapters 1–3 focus on two events from that period: (1) the fall of Samaria in 722 BCE, and (2) events surrounding the siege of Jerusalem in 701 BCE by the Assyrian king Sennacherib (705–681 BCE). Micah 1:5–7 specifically mentions Samaria’s destruction as a warning to Judah and Jerusalem that they will suffer the same fate if they do not change their behavior. These chapters do not explicitly mention the Assyrians, but they do condemn Judah’s behavior in a manner that anticipates Assyria’s subjugation of Judah and Jerusalem and culminates in Sennacherib’s siege. Both events likely occurred during the reign of Hezekiah (approximately 725–696 BCE).2 Even though the superscription of Micah (1:1) dates Micah’s prophetic activity during the reign of three Judean kings (Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah), scholars seldom date texts in the book to the time of Jotham or Ahaz. Instead, events in the reign of Hezekiah best account for the eighth-century materials in Micah (unless one accepts the date of the death of Ahaz as 715 BCE). These situations include the destruction of Samaria in 722 BCE and the siege of Sennacherib in 701 BCE. Knowledge of Samaria’s destruction serves a rhetorical function in 1:5–7 as a warning to Jerusalem. Later, in the last decade of the eighth century, Hezekiah attempts to consolidate resources and buttress his defenses in preparation for the anticipated attack from the Assyrians. These actions prove dangerous for villages in the Shephelah (the hilly region west of Jerusalem through which Sennacherib’s army would march on its way to Jerusalem). Micah 1:8–16 presents the prophet’s message of destruction for those villages.

Over the same time, during the reign of Hezekiah, Jerusalem itself nearly doubled in size. Various explanations for this expansion have been offered, including the arrival of refugees who fled to Jerusalem after the Assyrians defeated Samaria as well as broader population shifts caused by the upheaval of Assyrian rule in the Levant and its extensive policies of population exchanges.3 Hezekiah was king when Samaria fell to the Assyrians. During Hezekiah’s reign, the western hill of Jerusalem was populated, and reports in 2 Kgs 18–20 and 2 Chr 29–32 credit Hezekiah with major religious reforms and building projects. He extended the city wall and built the Siloam tunnel to provide a source of drinking water inside the city and to make the city less vulnerable to foreign military incursions.4 He also built storehouses for keeping supplies (though he undoubtedly received these supplies by taxing the population). He also fought with the Philistines, but his success against one Philistine king played a key role in convincing the Assyrian king that Hezekiah had rebelled against him (see below). The population expansions likely necessitated some of the building, but they also reflect Hezekiah’s policies of centralizing power in Jerusalem.

The situation in Jerusalem as portrayed in Mic 1–3 does not, however, focus attention on Hezekiah’s contributions to the city. Rather, Mic 1–3 critiques the nation for abandoning Yahweh (1:5–9) and for the injustice perpetrated by the wealthy over others. The bulk of chapters 2–3 condemns the greed of those wealthy elites of Judah and Jerusalem who schemed to take land and property from the rightful owners to line their own pockets. They took advantage of Hezekiah’s desire to enhance fortifications in Jerusalem and in Judah. Micah condemns “the heads of Jacob and the rulers of the house of Israel” for instigating such behavior (3:1). These chapters do not mention Hezekiah by name or even specify the king as responsible. One suspects, however, that such behavior either came on orders from the king or at the very least had his tacit support. This behavior leads the prophet to castigate the wealthy who use brute force to take advantage of the population (see 2:1–2, 8–9). The prophet also condemns the resulting situation of lawlessness that leads to bloodshed (3:1–3). In so doing, he takes aim at the political leaders (3:1, 9), prophets (3:5–7), and priests (3:11). Instead of working to stop the oppression, they take advantage of the situation to extract money for themselves. As a result, the early collection of Micah’s sayings climaxes with the pronouncement of Jerusalem’s destruction in 3:12 (editors likely also added comments in 1:5–7, 9, 12, 13 to explain Jerusalem’s destruction in the second phase).5





B. FROM SENNACHERIB’S SIEGE TO THE DESTRUCTION OF JERUSALEM


Micah 1–3 alludes frequently to Sennacherib’s siege of Jerusalem in 701 BCE.6 We possess four accounts of these events, but the details differ among them: three biblical accounts (2 Kgs 18:13–19:37; 2 Chr 32:1–22; Isa 36:1–37:38); and Sennacherib’s own account.7 The three biblical examples share a common source, but each account has been altered for its literary location.8 The basic outline begins with an unprovoked attack by Sennacherib that took the fortified cities of Judah and then turned toward Jerusalem. In the biblical accounts, the siege concludes with a divinely initiated plague among the Assyrians that forces them to withdraw.

Sennacherib’s account adds historical context, but it does not mention massive casualties to Assyrian troops. Sennacherib’s account attributes his decision to attack Judah to Hezekiah’s rebellion. It references Hezekiah’s capture of a Philistine king named Padi with whom Sennacherib had an alliance.9 Sennacherib claims to have withdrawn from Jerusalem only after Hezekiah paid him a large tribute. The Assyrian king allowed Hezekiah to remain in charge of Jerusalem, but Sennacherib reinstated Padi and divided Judean territory among three Philistine kings (including Padi) who had not revolted against him.

Following the lifting of Sennacherib’s siege of Jerusalem, Hezekiah remained king, but he ruled a much smaller kingdom. Sennacherib withdrew his forces from Jerusalem in 701 BCE. The biblical accounts claim that the Assyrians withdrew because Yahweh sent the angel of death against the Assyrians who killed 185,000 of Sennacherib’s soldiers (2 Kgs 19:35–37; Isa 37:36–38; cf. 2 Chr 32:21–23). Further, the biblical accounts imply that Sennacherib was killed immediately after he returned from his campaign against Jerusalem. In reality, while Sennacherib was eventually assassinated by two of his sons, he continued to rule for another twenty years after the siege of Jerusalem ended.

Hezekiah died early in the seventh century and was remembered in Judah for helping to save Jerusalem from the Assyrians. He was replaced by his son Manasseh (696–641 BCE), whose lengthy reign made him the longest ruling king in Judah and Israel. Nevertheless, the biblical assessments of Manasseh’s reign roundly condemn his actions as king (2 Kgs 21:1–18; 2 Chr 32:32–33:20). The theological assessment of Manasseh by the biblical writers does not credit him for stabilizing the political situation, but his lengthy reign suggests he made peace with the Assyrians. The writer of Kings condemns Manasseh for adopting Assyrian religious practices and styles that lead the people of Judah astray:

9But they did not listen; Manasseh misled them to do more evil than the nations had done that the LORD destroyed before the people of Israel. 10The LORD said by his servants the prophets, 11“Because King Manasseh of Judah has committed these abominations, has done things more wicked than all that the Amorites did, who were before him, and has caused Judah also to sin with his idols; 12therefore thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, I am bringing upon Jerusalem and Judah such evil that the ears of everyone who hears of it will tingle. 13I will stretch over Jerusalem the measuring line for Samaria, and the plummet for the house of Ahab; I will wipe Jerusalem as one wipes a dish, wiping it and turning it upside down. 14I will cast off the remnant of my heritage and give them into the hand of their enemies; they shall become a prey and a spoil to all their enemies, 15because they have done what is evil in my sight and have provoked me to anger, since the day their ancestors came out of Egypt, even to this day.” (2 Kgs 21:9–15 NRSV)

The length of his reign combined with the blame placed on him creates a dual conundrum that derives from the delay of divine punishment. Given the assessment of the writer of 2 Kgs 21:9, why did Yahweh wait so long to remove Manasseh? The writer of Kings leaves no doubt about Manasseh’s wickedness, but Manasseh ruled for fifty-five years during which time Yahweh could have removed Manasseh as king. Relatedly, Yahweh’s judgment pronouncement creates another problem. Given that this Kings account includes a prophetic oracle announcing that Manasseh caused Yahweh to decide to destroy Jerusalem (21:12–13), why does Yahweh not punish Jerusalem during Manasseh’s reign or immediately after his death? The destruction of Jerusalem does not happen for more than fifty years after Manasseh died. The Chronicler tries to solve the problem by eliminating 2 Kgs 21:10–15 (the prophetic judgment oracle) from his account and inserting a narrative detailing Manasseh’s radical conversion (2 Chr 33:11–17, 19).10

Manasseh’s son Amon takes the throne when Manasseh dies, but the king’s servants assassinated him after only two years (2 Kgs 21:18–26). He was replaced by Manasseh’s grandson Josiah (640–609 BCE). Only eight years old when he took the throne, Josiah becomes the paradigm of a pious king as described in Deut 17:14–20. In his eighteenth year, Josiah initiates a program of cultic, social, and political reforms after being presented with the Book of the Law found during renovation of the temple.11 Josiah died in 609 at the hands of the Egyptian pharaoh Neco II (610–595 BCE). The religious reforms of Josiah put a heavy emphasis upon covenant obligations, which also led to calls for more equitable social structures. Josiah’s political reforms intended to centralize power through Jerusalem and to reunite Judah with territories that had been part of the Northern Kingdom. After Josiah’s death, succeeding kings did not pursue the reforms as vigorously, but pockets of aristocrats, priests, and prophets continued to push for reforms.12

Following Josiah’s death, a rapid series of events resulted in a succession of four kings in twenty years. More importantly, each subsequent king took the throne due to the untimely departure of the previous king. Josiah was killed by the Egyptian pharaoh, Neco II, and Josiah’s son, Jehoahaz, took the throne in his stead. The kingship of Jehoahaz lasted only three months because the Egyptians (under Neco II) replaced Jehoahaz with another of Josiah’s sons, Eliakim, whom Neco gave the throne name Jehoiakim. Neco deported Jehoahaz to Egypt where he died (2 Kgs 23:34). Undoubtedly, Jehoiakim convinced the Egyptians that he would serve their interests, but Neco nevertheless forced Judah to pay tribute (2 Kgs 23:35).

In 605 BCE Babylon defeated Egypt at the Battle of Carchemish in Syria, under the command of Prince Nebuchadnezzar. He forced Egypt to withdraw back to its traditional borders, thereby ceding the Mediterranean coast to Babylon. The Babylonian king Nabopolassar died that same year, and his son became Nebuchadnezzar II, king of Babylon (604–562 BCE). Babylon consequently controlled the Mediterranean coastal lands, and Nebuchadnezzar probably returned two of the next three years to solidify his hold on the territory.13 Sources for this period are difficult to reconcile with one another. The Babylonian Chronicles note that Nebuchadnezzar stayed in Babylon at least one year to enhance his military capabilities, especially his chariots. The biblical texts present conflicting dates for Nebuchadnezzar’s deportations of Judeans from Jerusalem.

Texts

Nebuchadnezzar’s regnal year and event



2 Kgs 24:10–12

Year 8 (24:12)

First deportation (following Jehoiachin’s surrender)



2 Kgs 25:8

Year 19

Second deportation (Jerusalem destroyed)



2 Chr 36:9–21

No date given





Jer 52:12

Year 19

Second deportation (Jerusalem destroyed)



Jer 52:28–30

Year 7 (52:28)

First deportation (following Jehoiachin’s surrender)





Year 18 (52:29)

Second deportation (Jerusalem destroyed)





Year 23 (52:30)

Third deportation (after Gedaliah’s assassination)



While these dates cannot be reconciled, they do not differ that much. Despite the victory at Carchemish, Nebuchadnezzar never succeeded in his quest to conquer Egypt.

Egypt had taxed Judah heavily (2 Kgs 23:35), and Babylon continued to do the same. Jehoiakim complied but did so at great expense to “the people of the land,” the middle-class landowners, from whom he extracted the payments to the Babylonian king. For three years, Jehoiakim remained loyal to Nebuchadnezzar (2 Kgs 24:1), but then he decided to withhold tribute. Several countries staged rebellions when Nebuchadnezzar became king (a widespread practice), but eventually Nebuchadnezzar confronted Jehoiakim and laid siege to Jerusalem. Jehoiakim died during the siege when he was only thirty-six years old (2 Kgs 23:36), and his son Jehoiachin took over. Three months later, Jehoiachin surrendered to Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar then deports Jehoiachin to Babylon in 597 BCE where Jehoiachin lived as a prisoner until he died sometime after 560 (see 2 Kgs 25:27–28).14

Jehoiachin’s uncle, Zedekiah, was named king of Judah by Nebuchadnezzar II in 597 BCE. Zedekiah continued the line of Davidic descendants, but he undoubtedly had to convince the Babylonians that he would serve their interests. He did not, therefore, continue major portions of Josiah’s reforms. Ironically, within four years Zedekiah held a summit in Jerusalem attended by representatives of surrounding states. According to Jer 27, those attending included representatives of Edom, Moab, Ammon, and the Phoenician kings of Tyre and Sidon. Zedekiah hoped this summit would create an international force capable of overthrowing the Babylonians, but no formal action resulted from the conversations. It did, however, signal that Zedekiah had put Judah on a path of resistance to Babylonian control of Judah, resistance that would ultimately require Babylon to act against Judah. Zedekiah’s court remained divided over whether to acquiesce to Babylon or to seek help from Egypt. In the end, Zedekiah revolted against Babylon, and Nebuchadnezzar laid siege to Jerusalem (2 Kgs 24:20). Following the siege, Nebuchadnezzar razed the city by destroying the city wall and burning all the houses within the city, including the temple and the royal palace (2 Kgs 25:9–10; 2 Chr 36:19). Additionally, the Babylonians hauled away the temple furnishings and tools that had been covered with fine metals (gold, silver, and bronze). These valuable items were taken to Babylon where they were melted down and used to supplement the treasury of the Babylonians.





C. AFTER JERUSALEM’S DESTRUCTION


The destruction of Jerusalem in 587 BCE dramatically changed life in Jerusalem and Judah. The Babylonian conquest irreparably altered the physical and political landscape of the city. The Babylonians devastated the temple, the royal palace, and the city walls. The dynasty of Davidic kings who had ruled Judah from Jerusalem ceased to exist after more than four hundred years in power. The political leaders that supported the Judean monarchy were either killed, exiled, or forced to adapt to become vassals of the Babylonian Empire that occupied Judah. The temple, first constructed by David’s son Solomon in the tenth century, was demolished near the beginning of the sixth century. The complex structure of temple personnel who conducted the rituals were likewise set adrift or exiled to Babylon. Those who survived the Babylonian onslaughts of 597 and 587 all had to adapt. Those who were exiled included political leaders and temple personnel. Babylon did distinguish between the factions of Judean leadership that had supported continued relations with Babylon from those that hoped Egypt would provide military and economic support. The latter believed that Egypt would allow Judah to remain an independent kingdom. Many of the temple personnel supported Egypt, so most priests, Levites, and temple prophets in Jerusalem were exiled to Babylon.

The destruction of Jerusalem and its temple had a profound impact upon life in Judah, politically, socioeconomically, and theologically. For more than four hundred years, a descendant of David had ruled Judah as king (broken only by a seven-year period [841–835 BCE] when Queen Athaliah usurped the throne; see 2 Kgs 11; 2 Chr 22–23). The final two Judean kings, Jehoiachin and Zedekiah, were both exiled to Babylon, though Nebuchadnezzar brutally punished Zedekiah for his rebellion before sending him into exile.15 The administration of the kingdom was moved to Mizpah, where Gedaliah, a member of the family of Shaphan, was made administrator of the land. With the support of the Babylonians, he began to populate the farms with the poor from the land. This decision had the potential to change the social structure of Judah.16 He was, however, assassinated by Ishmael after serving only two months as administrator, so the policies he began to implement did not have time to play out.17 Yet, even without a temple, Judah’s ability to collect taxes did not suffer. With the support of Babylon, the economic importance of Mizpah continued until the Persians allowed exiles in Babylon to return to Jerusalem (beginning in 538 BCE). Gradually, over the next ninety years, Jerusalem again became the center of the province as Judeans rebuilt the temple (520–515 BCE) and restored the city walls (445 BCE).

Still, the theological emphases of the Zion tradition called for an explanation for Judah’s plight in 587. According to Zion theology, Yahweh chose Jerusalem as the place to establish his temple; he placed a descendant of David on the throne into perpetuity; and promised to protect Jerusalem from foreign nations. With the events of 587, all three pillars of Zion theology had failed. There was no longer a Davidide on the throne; Jerusalem lay in ruins; and Babylon demolished and looted the temple. Nevertheless, Zion theology did not die. It adapted.

The adaptation of the Zion tradition included changes to the texts we now have in the book of Micah, changes that increasingly spoke to those who remained in the land and to those who returned from exile in Babylon with a vision of rebuilding the temple. The content of Mic 4–7 responds to these changes in a series of additions (likely, first at Mizpah and later in the environs of the reconstructed city and temple of Jerusalem). First, chapters 6–7 clarify that Yahweh initiated the destruction of Jerusalem in response to poor leadership and the sins of the people of Judah. Second, 7:8–20 provides a message of hope that Yahweh has not abandoned the remnant that remained. Yahweh will act redemptively toward this remnant, just as Yahweh had brought Israel out of slavery in Egypt. Finally, someone compiled an extensive unit in chapters 4–5 that functions as a prophetic articulation of Yahweh’s future plan for Zion. These chapters anticipate Yahweh’s punishment and deliverance:

Writhe, and burst forth, Lady Zion, like the one giving birth,

but now you will go forth from a village

and you will dwell in a field,

and you will go to Babylon.

There you will be delivered.

And there Yahweh will redeem you from the hand of your enemy.

But now many nations will be gathered against you, saying,

“Let her be defiled, and let our eyes gaze on Zion.”

But they do not know the plans of Yahweh,

and they do not discern his counsel,

for he collects them like fallen grain on the threshing floor.

(Mic 4:10–12)

By placing chapters 4–5 in the book of Micah, with its eighth-century setting, editors insured that the readers understood that Yahweh reveals this plan to those who will listen. The later materials convey events that will happen in the future.18 Assyria and Babylon will fall, and Yahweh plans to make the nations subservient to Zion. For those living in the postexilic community, these words function as a promise on at least three levels. First, the content of these chapters speaks to Yahweh’s salvific intentions. Second, most of the sayings presume that either Yahweh or Yahweh’s designated prophet is the formal speaker. In either case, the speaker carries the weight of someone divinely sanctioned. Third, this divine sanction also enhances the trustworthiness of the promises themselves because the postexilic community knows the veracity of most of the promises already. The postexilic community can know that Assyria and Babylon have fallen. They recognize the claim as truthful that Yahweh punished Zion, but just as importantly, they know that people have begun returning from Babylon. By their own experience and knowledge, the remnant people know that Yahweh’s plans have so far unfolded as he said they would. Such knowledge, then, reinforces the belief that the remainder of the plan will also come about as Yahweh intends. While the eschatological formulas suggest this reconstitution of the glory of Zion will happen in the distant future when heard as a message from the eighth century, the postexilic community has the advantage of not living in the eighth century. They know what has already occurred and that knowledge provides comfort and confidence in Yahweh’s fidelity.





II. UNITY OF COMPOSITION


The book of Micah is a thoughtfully arranged collection of oracles and other compositions, but the content does not all come from the hand of the prophet from whom the book takes its name. Three or four major divisions are often noted: (1) the early core appearing in Mic 1–3, with its focus on events in the lifetime of the prophet, especially condemning the social inequity and cultic impropriety; (2) Mic 6–7, a composite block that begins with a trial speech condemning Judah’s guilt (6:1–7:7), followed by a series of speeches by different characters that express optimism that Judah will change its ways (7:8–20); and (3) chapters 4–5, which vacillate between judgment and hope, while looking to the more distant future.





A. THE EARLY CORE: FOCUS ON EIGHTH-CENTURY EVENTS


By most accounts, the early core of Micah appears in portions of chapters 1–3.19 This material highlights two thematic foci: the improper worship of deities other than Yahweh and ethical abuses (esp. the wealthy of Jerusalem and Judah taking advantage of those less well off). The biographic data in Mic 1:1 names Moresheth as the hometown of the prophet and lists three kings of Judah from the end of the eighth century BCE during which the prophet lived: Jotham (756–741 BCE), Ahaz (741–725 BCE), and Hezekiah (725–696 BCE). These dates imply that Micah was the youngest of the four eighth-century prophets (alongside Isaiah, Hosea, and Amos). In terms of content, Mic 1–3 presupposes two events from the late eighth century: the destruction of Samaria in 722 BCE and the siege of Sennacherib in 701 BCE (along with the royal centralization efforts leading up to the Assyrian incursion). The destruction of Samaria (see esp. 1:5–7, 9a, 12a) relates closely to the condemnation of the worship of deities other than Yahweh, while the bulk of Mic 2–3 condemns the actions of wealthy landowners in Judah and Jerusalem, who confiscated land to line their own pockets (esp. in the Shephelah).





B. SIXTH- AND FIFTH-CENTURY UPDATES


In response to the aftermath of Jerusalem’s destruction, proponents of Zion theology in the early exilic period placed the blame for Jerusalem’s destruction on the failure of the leaders and its people (see historical backgrounds above). Such is the case in the sixth-century texts added to Mic 1 and the way the chapter presents its message. Micah 1 castigates Jerusalem for following the Northern Kingdom practice of allowing sacrifices to gods other than Yahweh. This chapter repeatedly equates the religious behavior of Jerusalem to Samaria and classifies gifts to other deities as money paid to a harlot (Mic 1:5–7, 9a, 12b, 13b). In so doing, Mic 1 draws a parallel between the religious practices of the Northern and Southern Kingdoms for not worshiping Yahweh only. The harlotry language reflects influence of Hos 1–3 and the marriage metaphors that demand complete allegiance to Yahweh. The texts that articulate these points in Mic 1 appear to have been inserted into existing texts (1:5b, 9) or else took on new meaning after these insertions were added (1:12, 13). Elsewhere, 2 Kgs 17 articulates similar ideas by condemning Samaria for its worship of astral deities and Baal and by accusing Judah of the same behavior (2 Kgs 17:7–19).

Additionally, Mic 6–7 shows signs of having been added at the same time as the sixth-century additions to chapter 1 for a number of reasons. First, Mic 6–7 draws comparisons between Judah and Israel, as does Mic 1:5–7, 9, 12–13. Micah 6:16 also compares Jerusalem’s behavior to the policies of Omri and Ahab (see the mention of “the city” in 6:9, which assumes Jerusalem is the subject of the lawsuit). Omri and Ahab were both kings of the Northern Kingdom and were paradigms of evil in Kings (cf. 1 Kgs 16:25, 30, which claim first Omri and then Ahab was the worst king of Israel), especially since 1 Kgs 16:24 credits Omri for establishing the city of Samaria, and 1 Kgs 16:32 names Ahab as the king who built a temple for Baal in Samaria. This claim that Judah acted like Israel in the time of these kings thus comports well with the reference to the sins of Samaria that have reached the gates of Jerusalem in Mic 1:5–7, 9b, 12–13. Relatedly, the blending of references to “Israel” when referring to Judah and Jerusalem occurs in both places (1:5; 6:2, 9). Second, knowledge of other biblical texts includes Hosea and Amos in ways that assume the readers recognize that these two books condemn the Northern Kingdom.20 The hallmark of these sixth-century texts in Micah thus centers upon the need to blame the people and their leaders for the destruction of Jerusalem.

Chapters 6–7 also contain a prophetic complaint (7:1–7) and a Persian period salvific ending to the book (7:8–20) that presents a series of optimistic statements and responses regarding the fate of Zion. The prophetic complaint in 7:1–7 bemoans the disappearance of the faithful and the upright from Jerusalem. Micah 7:8–20 has often been classified as a liturgy because of the speaker and response style that develops across the verses. The climactic moment in the liturgy comes with the prophet’s intercessory prayer in 7:14–15a followed by Yahweh’s brief but positive promise to show his people marvelous deeds (7:15b). The people then proclaim their gratitude that Yahweh will protect them from the nations. This proclamation alludes to Yahweh’s compassion toward his people, despite the current punishment.





C. POSTEXILIC REFRAMING


The third block of texts to enter the book of Micah, as suggested in this commentary, includes the bulk of chapters 4–5. These chapters presuppose knowledge of the exile to Babylon (see esp. 4:10), and they address the concerns of the postexilic community in Jerusalem. As such, they deal with the role of the (restored) temple and the nations (4:1–5), the restoration of the remnant (4:6–7; 5:7–8), the return of the dominion of Zion (4:8–13), the continuation of the Davidic dynasty (5:1–6), and Yahweh’s removal of cultic improprieties (5:9–14). They also reflect an eschatological orientation for the future as signaled by the eschatological day formulas in 4:1, 6; 5:10.21 Hence, they do not come from the eighth century. The cumulative effect of these topics on the book characterizes Micah as a prophet in the vein of Isaiah, a prophet from the eighth century BCE whose book addresses the postexilic community.22

The role played by Mic 4–5 in addressing the postexilic community extends beyond the book of Micah as an isolated prophetic collection. These chapters play a significant role in the Book of the Twelve, both in terms of the topics they discuss and their location.23 The topics that speak to the postexilic community noted above can in many respects be understood as a reconstitution of the Zion tradition. As noted in the discussion of the exilic update, the destruction of Jerusalem in 587 undercuts the three main pillars of Zion theology. The topics in Mic 4–5 (unlike chs. 6–7) do not focus on who was to blame for Jerusalem’s destruction. Rather, chapters 4–5 present a hope for the future restoration of Zion (after Jerusalem’s destruction). They reiterate the role of Zion as Yahweh’s chosen city, the role of David’s descendants as Yahweh’s chosen leaders, and Yahweh’s protection of Jerusalem from foreign nations. The nations in Mic 4–5 make a pilgrimage to Zion to learn torah and to hear the word of Yahweh (4:1–4). In the end of days (4:1), Zion will again serve as the mountain of Yahweh and home to Yahweh’s temple (4:2), and peace will reign (4:3). Zion’s realm will be restored (4:4–13), and David’s descendants will rule Israel as they had done in David’s lifetime (5:1–3). The kingdom will survive Assyrian aggression, and Yahweh will use the remnant of Jacob that has been exiled among the nations to defeat those nations (5:4–8). On that day, Yahweh will remove all the cultic maladies that had previously afflicted the country (5:9–14).

The location of these chapters that articulate the long-term vision for Zion is also no accident. Micah 4 begins immediately following Mic 3:12, a climactic verse for the early collection of Mic 1–3. That verse also manifests a marginal note from the Masoretes identifying the verse as the exact middle of the Twelve if one is counting by verses. The thematic juxtaposition of Jerusalem’s destruction in 3:12 followed immediately by the utopian message that the nations will stream to the city to learn torah and hear the word of Yahweh could hardly be more jarring. The eschatological orientation of the promise pushes boldly into the future when the action implies Yahweh has a plan to establish peace and security in the land.

These chapters also raise questions. While the content reflects a postexilic setting, one cannot help but wonder whose vision these chapters represent. By most accounts they have a very different message for Jerusalem than either the core collection (that appears mostly in chs. 1–3) or the exilic update (chs. 6–7) that seeks to lay blame for Jerusalem’s destruction upon the leaders and the people who turned away from exclusive worship of Yahweh. By contrast, the message of Mic 4–5 conveys a strong sense of hope in Yahweh and conveys little fear concerning the nations. What, then, can one say about the identity of the author(s) of this postexilic block of texts? Recent suggestions have highlighted the likelihood that a group of scribal prophets are responsible for shaping the books comprising the Latter Prophets.24 These works stress the importance of scribal education in composing these collections. Prior to Jerusalem’s destruction, major scribal projects were funded by the king, but in the postexilic period, the temple became the funding source for such projects.25 Over time, collections of prophetic texts were compiled, and the scribes who compiled the Twelve incorporated several distinctive ideas into the collection. These conceptual elements include at least the following: a chronological structure that runs from the eighth century to the Persian period; recurring use of the concept of the day of Yahweh to anticipate Yahweh’s intervention in the affairs of Judah, Israel, and the nations; the fertility of the land as a sign of the covenant curse or blessing; the fate of God’s people over time as a means of stressing the need for obedience to Yahweh; and dealing with the problem of theodicy.26

The assumption that Mic 4–5 derives from scribal conversations concerning Yahweh’s plans for his chosen people over a lengthy chronological period helps one understand the purpose of the Twelve as a collection and Micah’s role therein as a vehicle for expressing theological convictions that were considered important. Highlights include a range of affirmations in these chapters: an emphasis upon Zion as the place of instruction (torah) and the word of Yahweh (prophecy) for Yahweh’s people and the nations (4:2); the dual foci on the centrality of the temple and a reassertion of the theological pillars of the Zion tradition (described above); a positive attitude toward the nations (4:1–5) that counterbalances the expectations that the nations will still represent a force that will need to be subdued (note the anticipation of Assyrian empirical rule in 5:5–6, 7–8, 15); the need for cultic purification is anticipated (5:9–14). The scrolls of the four Latter Prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the Twelve), as a group, came to carry considerable weight in explaining Judah’s situation after the reconstruction of Jerusalem and the temple.27 By most reckonings, the Prophets became recognized as an authoritative collection of scrolls not long after the Torah takes shape, and the significance of these scrolls for helping to shape the identity of the postexilic community should not be underestimated.28





III. AUTHORSHIP AND PLACE OF ORIGIN


The book of Micah sets its sights on the faith community of Jerusalem and Judah, though the prophet for whom the book is named was born in the Shephelah, specifically in a village called Moresheth (Mic 1:1; Jer 26:18) or Moresheth-Gath (Mic 1:14). Most scholars identify this village as Tell-el-Judeideh, an ancient town located a little more than twenty miles southwest of Jerusalem.29 The territory of the Shephelah was often disputed territory between Judah and the Philistines, and Hezekiah’s capture of a Philistine king, Padi, certainly exacerbated those strained relationships (see the discussion of the historical backgrounds above). The mention of Moresheth-Gath appears in a unit (1:9–16) that warns a number of cities in the Shephelah regarding the danger they will face when the Assyrians decide to destroy them on their way to Jerusalem. In fact, the Assyrian king Sennacherib claims to have destroyed forty-six fortified cities in Judah during his march against Jerusalem. He then laid siege to Jerusalem but was unable to destroy it. While the biblical accounts emphasize the miraculous delivery of Jerusalem from the siege, Sennacherib’s account claims victory. Sennacherib claims he only lifted the siege because Hezekiah paid him a large bounty to leave. In addition, Sennacherib divided up most of Hezekiah’s Judean territory among the Philistine kings of Ashdod, Ekron, and Gaza, who were loyal to him.

The charges leveled against Jerusalem in Mic 1–3 include cultic infidelity and ethical abuses. These charges culminate in the pronouncement of judgment against Jerusalem in Mic 3:12. Micah 1 focuses on the charge of Jerusalem’s cultic infidelity, including offering gifts to deities other than Yahweh (1:7–8, 9, 12). These accusations accentuate their problem by associating Jerusalem’s sins with emulating the infidelity of Samaria (1:5, 9, 12), the capital city of the Northern Kingdom destroyed by the Assyrians in 722. This charge of cultic infidelity takes up language from Hosea and Amos (see the commentary on Mic 1:7), and this allegation resonates with the condemnations against the Northern Kingdom that appear repeatedly in the book of Kings following the cessation of Israel from Judah in the reign of Jeroboam I (926–906 BCE). Jeroboam established two rival temples (one in Bethel and one in Dan) to discourage the citizens of Israel from sacrificing at the temple in Jerusalem. This action becomes a major issue in Kings to explain the severity of Jeroboam’s decision (since Yahweh chose Jerusalem as the site of his temple [see Deut 12:5, 11–14; 1 Kgs 8:12–21]).30

The bulk of chapters 2–3 focuses less on covenant fidelity than in chapter 1. Instead, they chastise Judah’s leadership for making Jerusalem into a city of bloodshed (3:10), injustice (3:8–9, 10), and violence perpetrated against other Judeans (2:8–9; 3:2–3). Those who receive special condemnation from the prophet do not constitute the general populace of society but its social, political, and religious elite. The condemnation is particularly harsh for the powerful (2:1), those gaining wealth at the expense of others (2:2), the civic leaders (3:1, 9), priests (3:11) and prophets (3:5–6, 11). The prophet condemns these for failing to do good, and seeking evil (2:1, 3; 3:2).

Given what we know about Hezekiah, it is not difficult to associate the references to the powerful scheming to evict people from their houses with the king’s plans to confiscate land to improve military defenses. The improvement of fortifications of cities in the Shephelah was designed to slow the expected incursion of the Assyrian king. These actions, however, did little to slow Sennacherib on his way to Jerusalem since he claims to have destroyed forty-six of Judah’s fortified cities on his campaign.31

The unethical means for procuring properties for the king’s building plans is not the only charge leveled against the elite of the city. The prophet condemned organized bands of robbers who ambushed those going about their business (2:8); and leaders who charge money for their work as rulers (3:11; 7:3), judges (7:3), priests (3:11), and prophets (3:5–7, 11).

Such charges are no less pointed in the later material of chapters 4–7. The bulk of the accusations appear in the trial scene of Mic 6. Yahweh serves as the prosecuting attorney, and accuses Jacob/Israel of lying, violence, unethical business practices (see 6:10–12), as well as following the lead of the two worst kings of the Northern Kingdom (Omri and Ahab). In addition, Yahweh pronounces judgment upon the nations in general (4:11–13; 5:8–9, 15; 7:13, 16); as well as specific reference to Assyria (5:5–6; 7:8–10), Egypt (7:12), and Babylon (7:12).





IV. THE TEXT OF MICAH


The text of Micah, like most of the Book of the Twelve, reflects a relatively stable Hebrew transmission, though it is not without its complexities. These problems, however, typically revolve around questions of comprehension regarding the unpointed, poetic text on the part of scribes and translators. The text of Micah, unlike that of Jeremiah or Ezekiel, does not exhibit significant pluses or minuses when compared to early manuscript traditions in Hebrew and Greek.

Recognition of a stable Hebrew textual transmission does not mean the text of the MT, the Septuagint, the Qumran fragments, and other texts from the Judean Desert provide identical readings. They do not. The differences, however, can generally be traced to attempts by early scribes and translators to improve, or at least make intelligible, passages that remain difficult to understand.

Some differences almost certainly occur in the act of translation of the unpointed text. Three examples illustrate this tendency. First, the name of the town in Mic 1:14, Achzib (ʾakzîb), refers to a small village just under twenty miles south and west of Jerusalem during the time of Micah. The message of 1:14 creates a pun between that town’s name and the similar sounding Hebrew word for deception (ʾakzāb) which is the next word in 1:14. The Greek translator apparently missed the pun, and instead of translating ʾakzîb as the name of the town he uses two different Greek adjectives meaning “frivolous” or “useless.”32 The first one functions as an attributive adjective (mataios, “frivolous”) modifying houses, and the second adjective (kena, “useless”) functions as the subject of the verbless clause. As a result, where the Hebrew reads “the houses of Achzib will be a deception” the Greek translator renders the clause as “frivolous houses will become useless.” The statement thus reads quite differently in Greek and Hebrew, but the Greek still reflects the unpointed Hebrew text and attempts to make sense of the phrase for a Greek-speaking audience.

A second example of changes caused by translation can be found in 6:10, where the three Hebrew consonants hʾš are pointed in the MT as an interrogative h followed by a particle (ʾiš) meaning “Is there?” By contrast, the Greek understands the same three letters as the definite article (h) attached to the noun ʾêš, so that the Hebrew word means “the fire.” Given that the translator worked from an unpointed Hebrew text, and that the word “fire” is much more common than the particle, one can recognize that the Septuagint reads the consonants quite differently, but still translates the same unpointed Hebrew consonants.

Not every variation can be as clearly attributed to the translator, but enough of these deviations exist that one can extrapolate this tendency as part of the translation process for the translator of the Book of the Twelve.33 Interestingly, while dozens of variants in ancient Greek translations manifest this tendency to modify the text so that it makes better sense, the same cannot be said concerning variations in the Hebrew manuscripts of the Twelve from the Judean Desert. To date, at least four partial copies of Hebrew versions of Micah exist in some form.34 None of these manuscripts contain a complete copy of Micah. These manuscripts are fragmented, often containing only a few words on a line, but some manuscripts appear in scrolls with other writings from the Twelve.35 Cumulatively the Hebrew manuscripts cover portions of virtually every verse in Micah (and many verses appear in more than one manuscript).36 One must, of course, evaluate each variant reading on its own merit since the manuscripts date from the second century BCE to the second century CE. Nevertheless, the cumulative impression strongly suggests that by 150 BCE, the unpointed text of Micah was quite stable.

The Greek manuscript of the Twelve found at Nahal Hever, 8Ḥev 1, offers a third example regarding the way that translation differences can actually point to the stability of the unpointed Hebrew text of Micah. This Greek manuscript dates to the first century CE. Like many of the scrolls from Qumran and the Judean Desert, the manuscript is more a series of fragments than a full scroll, so only portions of Micah are extant in this manuscript (and nothing after Mic 5:6).37 In places, it differs significantly from the Old Greek translation of the Septuagint, but the differences, by and large, reflect an alternative translation of the same unpointed Hebrew text that forms the basis of MT. This Greek manuscript, nevertheless, adds significantly to the ancient witnesses from Qumran and the Judean Desert. Consider Mic 5:4(3) as a case in point. The MT of Mic 5:4 is not attested in any of the fragments of ancient Hebrew manuscripts found at Qumran or the fragments of Twelve Prophets found at Wadi Murabba’at.38 It does appear, however, in the Twelve Prophets scroll found at Nahal Hever (8Ḥev 1), which confirms the verse was not a late addition to the text of Micah. The Greek text of this verse in 8Ḥev 1 differs considerably, however, from the version that forms the basis of the Septuagint. In fact, Mic 5:4 differs more significantly from the Septuagint version than it does from MT.

Mic 5:4(3)

Underlining denotes a difference between the LXX and 8Ḥev 1. Asterisks ***** in the column with the transliteration of 8Ḥev 1 indicate Greek words are missing from 8Ḥev 1 when compared with the LXX.

MT: And he will stand and shepherd in the strength of Yahweh, in the pride of the name of Yahweh his God, and thus they will dwell, for now, he will be magnified to the end of the earth.

LXX:

8Ḥev 1 (8ḤevXII gr)



kai stēsetai kai opsetai kai poimanei

to poimnion autou

kai en tē doxē tou onomatos kyriou tou theou autōn

hyparxousin dioti nun

megalynthēsetai

heōs akrōn tēs gēs.

kai [st]ēsetai kai ******* *** poimanei

***********

en ischui YHWH ()

kai en tē eparsei *** onomatos YHWH () theou [autōu]

kai epistraphēsontai oti nun

megal[ynthē]sontai

heōs peratōn tēs gēs.



LXX Translated:

And he shall stand and see and shepherd

***********

in the strength of the Lord (kyrios)

and in the glory of the name of the Lord their God they shall exist,

for now, he shall be magnified to the ends of the earth,

8Ḥev 1 Translated:

And he shall stand and shepherd

in the strength of YHWH ()

and in the pride of the name of YHWH () his God they shall return

since now, they shall be magnified to the extremities of the earth



When one compares the Septuagint version with the MT and with 8Ḥev 1, several things stand out. First, the LXX has an additional verb not present in the other two texts, but it is not clear that the Septuagint translator worked from a different source text. The verbs opsetai (LXX only) and poimanei retrovert back to two Hebrew homonyms which are spelled differently but pronounced very similarly. The verb opsetai retroverts back to the Hebrew rʾh (with an aleph) and means “to see,” while the Greek word poimanei retroverts back to rʿh (with an ayin) and means “to pasture” or “to shepherd.” Second, the Septuagint offers a translation that is not word for word with the Hebrew (kai poimanei to poimnion autou), which means “he shall pasture his flock.” The words “his flock” (to poimnion autou) are not attested in MT or 8Ḥev 1. This more paraphrastic translation thus adds a noun (poimnion) from the same verbal form that appears in both the LXX and 8Ḥev 1 (poimanei). The addition of the noun arguably makes better sense stylistically of the Hebrew clause. The Greek text in 8Ḥev 1 simply translates literally, using the same Greek verb as the LXX (poimanei), but without the noun form functioning as a direct object (with the resulting text aligning closely with MT: “He shall shepherd in the strength of his Lord”). In so doing, 8Ḥev 1 uses one Greek word for one Hebrew word, but the resulting Greek seems stilted in comparison to the LXX.

Third, the text in 8Ḥev 1 translates the unpointed Hebrew word “wyšbw” as epistraphēsontai (meaning “they shall return” or “they shall bring back”), while the LXX translates the Hebrew with hyparxousin (typically meaning, “They will exist”). 8Ḥev 1 therefore understands wyšbw as coming from the root šûb. By contrast the LXX appears to understand the Hebrew (along with the MT) as coming from the root yšb, meaning “to sit,” or “to dwell.” The Greek word used by the LXX (hyparxousin) is not used elsewhere in the Old Testament to translate yšb, but the LXX translator of Jer 4:14 uses hyparxousin to translate the Hebrew root lûn (which means “to lodge” or “dwell”). Clearly, then the range of meanings of hyparxousin includes the idea of habitation, as can yšb (cf. Gen 4:20; 36:20), so when retroverted this Greek word points back to the same Hebrew consonants as the MT (from the root yšb). The Hebrew syntax is also quite cumbersome. The implication is clear: Despite the very different meanings of Greek words in the LXX and 8Ḥev 1, both translations interpret the same unpointed Hebrew text. When all of these issues are taken into account, one must conclude that the two Greek translators simply tried to make sense of the same unpointed Hebrew text that manifests a complex syntactical construction.

Fourth, the LXX consistently translates the name Yahweh with the noun kyrios (Lord), a practice mirrored by most modern English translations that translate Yahweh as the LORD—using small capital letters to distinguish it from ʾadônai which is also translated as “Lord” (where only the first letter is written as a capital letter). By contrast, the Greek manuscript of 8Ḥev 1 treats the name differently, by both transliterating the Tetragrammaton in unpointed Hebrew and by using an archaic Hebrew script () so that the name YHWH stands out graphically from the Greek words surrounding it.39 The Tetragrammaton has a complex history, but each of the three texts has a similar aim to recognize that the name Yahweh should be treated with special reverence. The MT uses the vowel pointing for ʾadônai (“Lord”) whenever the word YHWH appears, to remind anyone reading the text not to pronounce the name of God. The LXX uses the Greek noun kyrios, which reflects the same practice as the MT. In 8Ḥev 1, the numinous quality of Yahweh’s name is signified by the use of the archaic script.

Fifth, several words are merely synonyms of one another or suggest a stylistic choice by the translator. Such cases do not suggest a different Hebrew word than what appears in the MT. The use of akrōn by the LXX and peratōn by 8Ḥev 1 both mean “extremities” or “ends.” As such, both words offer a valid translation of the Hebrew ʾapsê in the MT. Relatedly, while the LXX uses dioti and 8Ḥev 1 uses oti in the lines above, both words translate the Hebrew conjunction kî. The LXX typically uses dioti, but in Mic 1:9, where two examples of ky appear in the Hebrew, the LXX translates one with dioti and one with oti.

Finally, when writing up text notes in the commentary this kind of evaluation creates a dilemma. A complete description of all text-critical variants becomes prohibitive for reasons of space. As a result, one must make subjective decisions concerning which variants are important enough to mention in the text-critical notes and which ones do not find their way into the text-critical notes. For the sake of transparency, I mention some of the principles I tried to follow in an effort to document consistently. I have endeavored to be as thorough as possible in highlighting variants, though I may have missed a few. I attempted to err on the side of inclusion because both the similarities and the differences among the various ancient manuscripts do two things simultaneously. They highlight the stability of the unpointed text of the Twelve and demonstrate a certain fluidity in the copying and translation of texts, even biblical texts, in the ancient world. Printing presses did not yet exist, so copying errors can be common, but the surprisingly few differences among the ancient manuscripts compared to the unpointed consonants of the MT speak to the care with which these documents were copied.40 Nevertheless, complete discussion of every textual variant would dramatically lengthen these text notes, without necessarily enhancing one’s understanding of the meaning of the text. I have included variants that only concern Greek translations, even though they do not suggest a different Hebrew Vorlage than the unpointed text of the MT. These include instances of Greek synonyms that do not point to a different Hebrew text.

I also kept an eye out for purely morphological variants that can exist in some texts. For example, in unpointed manuscripts from texts in Qumran and the Judean Desert, the Hebrew conjunction ky can be spelled with two letters (ky as in the MT) or with three letters (the plene spelling kyʾ as in the Habakkuk Pesher). This particular spelling difference does not, however, occur in the extant manuscripts containing text from Micah. One prominent morphological difference does appear in two manuscripts, specifically the use of the paleo-Hebrew script when writing the name Yahweh in the Greek translation of 8Ḥev 1 discussed above and in the Hebrew text of 8Ḥev 1 (= 1QpMic). I have not, however, created a text note for every instance where this happens.

This kind of textual analysis of potential variants can be tedious to some (although I find such issues utterly fascinating to ponder), but limits have had to be set. Some may disagree with my decisions on certain variants. Nevertheless, I trust that the text-critical notes that do appear will provide a window into the fascinating work of ancient scribes who often modified the works they copied according to their own agendas.41

Scribes generally approached the task of copying the scrolls seriously, and in the case of extant manuscripts of Micah, the evidence suggests they largely succeeded in recording the text accurately. In cases where translators took some degree of liberty, one can only say in their defense that many of these same passages continue to confound translators today. That lack of clarity does not, however, suggest the translators were working with a text significantly different from MT in the case of Micah.





V. READING MICAH IN THE TWELVE


The book of Micah plays an important role in the structure and message of the Twelve.42 This statement recognizes several issues simultaneously. First, the statement assumes that readers know that “the Twelve” functions as a name given in antiquity to the collection of twelve prophetic writings (Hosea–Malachi) that were small enough to be copied on a single scroll. Second, in some way, this collection was not only copied together; it also came to be counted as one of the four scrolls comprising the Latter Prophets. Third, the opening statement of this paragraph assumes that the order in which these twelve prophetic writings occur is not arranged haphazardly. Rather, the sequence of these writings represents an intentional arrangement that became fixed over time.43

In the MT (and English Bibles), Micah appears as the sixth book. Just as importantly, it appears as the third and final prophetic collection in the Twelve whose superscription dates the prophet to the eighth century. The superscriptions in Hosea, Amos, and Micah list eighth-century kings in a patterned sequence that links these three prophets whose prophetic activity overlaps, and the last king mentioned in Mic 1:1 (Hezekiah) is also named as great-great-grandfather of the prophet in Zeph 1:1. The pattern includes Jeroboam II for Hosea and Amos because those writings primarily address the Northern Kingdom:



Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, Hezekiah ruled Judah 786–696 BCE;

Josiah ruled from 639–608 BCE;

Jeroboam II was king of the Northern Kingdom 786–746 BCE,

roughly contemporary with Uzziah.

These superscriptions help to provide the Twelve with a chronological profile, along with superscriptions in Haggai and Zechariah 1–8. These six writings that mention kings essentially extend across the eighth, seventh, and sixth centuries in that order.44 Four of the remaining six writings owe their position in the Twelve to chronological considerations.45

The eighth century played an important role in Judean thought well into the postexilic period regarding the role of Assyria as an empire in relation to Judah’s worship of Yahweh. Three texts provide some context regarding the intellectual background against which one can understand Micah’s inclusion and sequence: Neh 9:32; 2 Kgs 17; and Isa 10.46 Nehemiah 9:32 demonstrates the sense in which the return from exile to Judah did not mean that life in Judah suddenly fulfilled all the aspiration of those who returned from exile and those who remained in the land. This verse appears as part of the prayer of Ezra in the book of Nehemiah (which recounts events from 445 BCE) wherein Ezra implores Yahweh to stop punishing Judah:

Now therefore, our God—the great and mighty and awesome God, keeping covenant and steadfast love—do not treat lightly all the hardship that has come upon us, upon our kings, our officials, our priests, our prophets, our ancestors, and all your people, since the time of the kings of Assyria until today. (NRSV)

The reference to the “kings of Assyria” who have inflicted hardship upon the Judeans almost certainly implies events from the eighth century. The expansion of the Assyrian Empire westward into the kingdoms of Judah and Israel happened at that time. Hence, Ezra’s prayer reflects the idea that Yahweh punished Judah because the people and their leaders broke faith with Yahweh (Neh 9:32–33). Ezra’s petition admits that “our kings, our officials, our priests, our ancestors, and all your people” (9:32, cf. 9:34) have “acted wickedly” (9:33), but it also implores Yahweh for mercy.

In addition, 2 Kgs 17 shares ideas with Mic 1:2–5, 9, 12; namely, that Yahweh punished Israel before Judah, and that by sending the Assyrians to capture Israel, Judah should heed this action as Yahweh’s warning:

7This occurred because the people of Israel had sinned against the LORD their God, who had brought them up out of the land of Egypt from under the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt. They had worshiped other gods 8and walked in the customs of the nations whom the LORD drove out before the people of Israel, and in the customs that the kings of Israel had introduced. 9The people of Israel secretly did things that were not right against the LORD their God. They built for themselves high places at all their towns, from watchtower to fortified city; 10they set up for themselves pillars and sacred poles on every high hill and under every green tree; 11there they made offerings on all the high places, as the nations did whom the LORD carried away before them. They did wicked things, provoking the LORD to anger; 12they served idols, of which the LORD had said to them, “You shall not do this.” 13Yet the LORD warned Israel and Judah by every prophet and every seer, saying, “Turn from your evil ways and keep my commandments and my statutes, in accordance with all the law that I commanded your ancestors and that I sent to you by my servants the prophets.” 14They would not listen but were stubborn, as their ancestors had been, who did not believe in the LORD their God. (2 Kgs 17:7–14 NRSV)

This passage delineates the sins of Israel in much greater detail than Neh 9, and it also contains an implicit warning to Judah (17:13–14), as well as an explicit statement that Judah was also guilty: “Judah also did not keep the commandments of the LORD their God but walked in the customs that Israel had introduced” (2 Kgs 17:19 NRSV).

Finally, Isa 10 sheds light on another aspect of thought about Assyrian kings and their relationship to Judah and Israel. In the context of Isaiah, chapter 9 ends with Yahweh expressing frustration at the inability of Judah and Israel to return to Yahweh. Yahweh has sent punishment in the form of adversaries (Syria to the east and the Philistines to the west in Isa 9:12, while Ephraim and Judah battled each other according to 9:21a). These initiatives, however, did not succeed, and the narrator comments that Yahweh needed to increase pressure against Israel and Judah: “For all this his anger has not turned away; his hand is stretched out still” (9:21b). At the end of Isa 9, Yahweh decides to find a more powerful nation by whom to punish Israel and Judah.

Isaiah 10 expresses both Yahweh’s decision to send Assyria and to limit what the king of Assyria can do. Yahweh delivers a speech that states Yahweh’s own people have become a “godless nation,” and that Yahweh intends to punish them as a result. On the one hand, Yahweh commands Assyria whom he names as “the rod of my anger” (10:5):

5Ah, Assyria, the rod of my anger—the club in their hands is my fury! 6Against a godless nation I send him, and against the people of my wrath I command him, to take spoil and seize plunder, and to tread them down like the mire of the streets. (10:5–6 NRSV)

Further, Yahweh will wield Assyria as a “rod.” Yahweh will, however, command Assyria to punish Judah as a godless nation. Yet, Yahweh also states that the Assyrian king has bigger ambitions that Yahweh will not allow him to accomplish:

7But this is not what he [i.e., the king of Assyria] intends, nor does he have this in mind; but it is in his heart to destroy, and to cut off nations not a few…. 12When the Lord has finished all his work on Mount Zion and on Jerusalem, he will punish the arrogant boasting of the king of Assyria and his haughty pride.

Yahweh describes the extent of the evil that the king of Assyria intends (see the details in 10:8–11), but that Yahweh will also punish the king of Assyria once Assyria has defeated Yahweh’s people. The punishment of Assyria will take place at a time of Yahweh’s choosing, once Yahweh has punished Judah and Jerusalem (10:12): “When the Lord has finished all his work on Mount Zion and on Jerusalem, he will punish the arrogant boasting of the king of Assyria and his haughty pride.” Yahweh quotes the king of Assyria who mistakenly believes he controls how much damage he can inflict. Yahweh responds with a judgment oracle against Assyria’s king that begins with a rhetorical question taunting the king’s erroneous ideas:

15Shall the ax vaunt itself over the one who wields it, or the saw magnify itself against the one who handles it? As if a rod should raise the one who lifts it up, or as if a staff should lift the one who is not wood! 16Therefore the Sovereign, the LORD of hosts, will send wasting sickness among his stout warriors, and under his glory a burning will be kindled, like the burning of fire. (Isa 10:15–16 NRSV)

Yahweh thus leaves no doubt: Yahweh alone will determine how Israel and Judah’s punishment will take shape (using Assyria as the rod to punish Israel and Judah), but Yahweh will send sickness upon the warriors of the Assyrian king (which certainly forms an apt description of the end of Sennacherib’s siege in the biblical versions).

Reading Micah in the Twelve assumes that one recognizes similar dynamics at play in Micah, but Micah also exhibits its own distinctive emphases that likely arose from the lengthy compositional process, as well as its context in the MT’s Hebrew order, where the books on either side (Jonah and Nahum) also center Yahweh’s determination of the fate of Assyria. With 2 Kgs 17, Micah shares the view that Yahweh’s decision to destroy Samaria, while delaying the destruction of Jerusalem, manifests clear affinities with the critique of the Northern Kingdom that runs throughout the book of Kings following the rebellion led by Jeroboam I (926–906 BCE) as recounted in 1 Kgs 12. The book of Kings blames several other kings of Israel for allowing the worship of Baal, the establishment of high places, and the use of idols. The book of Kings also blames all of the rulers of Israel for following “the sin(s) of Jeroboam.”47 That being said, these thematic affinities do not reflect the precise wording of the critiques of the Northern Kingdom in the book of Kings. With Isa 10, the book of Micah shares the conviction that Yahweh will punish the Assyrians following a time of punishment for Judah, though Micah goes beyond Isa 10 to anticipate Yahweh’s people will rule over Assyria and other nations (cf. Mic 5:6–7; 7:8–13; Isa 10:12, 16–17). Micah and Neh 9:32 contribute to a sense of delay that Judah’s people will experience before Assyria’s punishment comes. Both Micah and Isa 10 anticipate a lengthy period of Assyrian domination by using the formula “on that day” (Mic 4:6; 5:10; 7:11–12; Isa 10:20, 27) to connote that the time of restoration for Yahweh’s remnant people lies well in the future. Micah frontloads discussion of the theme of judgment against Yahweh’s people and the eventual punishment of the nations (including Assyria and Babylon) in chapters 4–7, but Micah exhibits stronger eschatological overtones. Judah will have to wait until the distant future (cf. also “the end of days” in Mic 4:1).

Whereas Mic 4–7 reflects awareness of a lengthy period of subjugation by Assyria, Jonah and Nahum (the books on either side of Micah in the Twelve) both concern Yahweh’s dealings with Nineveh (the capital of Assyria) as the primary subject of Yahweh’s activity. Nevertheless, the fate of Nineveh in Jonah and Nahum could hardly be more different. In Jonah, Yahweh sends the prophet to preach against Nineveh (the capital of Assyria). Jonah does not want to go and so he flees in the exact opposite direction. Yahweh, however, forces Jonah to deliver the message to Nineveh. Upon hearing Jonah’s reluctant delivery of arguably the shortest prophetic judgment speech in the entire Bible, the people of Nineveh repent dramatically, followed by the king, even more dramatically (Jonah 3:4–9).48 The king of Nineveh (in Jonah 3:9) even uses the words of Joel 2:14 to express hope that Yahweh might change his mind. In fact, when God saw how the Ninevites turned away from doing evil, Yahweh did change his mind and decided not to send calamity upon them. Yahweh’s penchant for compassion irritates Jonah to no end, and Jonah even tells Yahweh that is why he did not want to deliver Yahweh’s message (Jonah 4:2). In the end, Nineveh repents and survives through Yahweh’s grace, and Jonah looks petty.

The book of Nahum, by contrast, offers no reprieve for Nineveh. From the beginning of the book to the end, Nahum pronounces the imminent destruction of Nineveh. The book begins with a superscription (1:1) that explicitly names Nineveh as the subject of this prophetic writing. A hymn follows immediately that states Yahweh will destroy his enemies (1:2–3), and the remainder of Nah 1 leaves no doubt that Nineveh counts as one of Yahweh’s enemies. Nahum 2–3 consist of lengthy descriptive material concerning Nineveh’s looming downfall and disgrace.

Modern interpreters were by no means the first to notice the very different messages conveyed by Jonah and Nahum concerning Assyria. In fact, several ancient interpreters argue that Jonah’s trek occurred first, and they speculated that the deliverance of Nineveh is best explained in conversation with Nahum. Since the deliverance of Nineveh in Jonah was based on the Assyrians’ change of behavior regarding their penchant for evil, these ancient interpreters assumed that after Jonah, Assyria reverted to its old ways.49 In some important ways, Micah provides the linchpin connecting the deliverance of Nineveh in Jonah and Nineveh’s destruction in Nahum because, in Micah, the Assyrians act with malice toward Judah and they destroy Samaria. Jonah makes clear that Yahweh had used a prophet (even a reluctant one) to pronounce judgment as an implicit warning that Assyria heeded. Just like the prophetic messages Yahweh commissioned to Judah and Israel, however, Yahweh’s mercy at one point in time does not preclude judgment will not be inflicted at a later point. Prophetic messages of doom carry an implicit call to change, and prophetic messages of salvation were contingent upon remaining in Yahweh’s good graces. These theological convictions, in fact, likely account for the consistency with which prophetic books were ultimately structured by alternating words of judgment (which always begin prophetic writings) with words of hope (which conclude most prophetic collections).50

The role of Assyria in Micah does not, however, constitute the only “conversation” in which Micah participates with the other books in the Twelve. The fate of Israel and Judah represents an even greater thematic concern in Micah than the role of Assyria. This topic plays a major role in all four prophetic collections, not just the Twelve. One objection to taking seriously the role of the Twelve as a literary and canonical entity has been that modern work on the Twelve relies too heavily upon theories of redactional shaping of the individual books versus what one can “prove” using early manuscripts from the Judean Desert where the twelve books lack a title for the collection as a whole.51 The problem with this reasoning is that the earliest manuscripts date to the middle of the second century BCE, while the earliest reference to the Twelve prophets appears in Sir 49:10, some thirty to fifty years before the earliest Judean Desert texts. This early reference in Sirach already presumes that the Twelve constitute a prophetic book alongside Isaiah (Sir 48:20), Jeremiah (Sir 49:6), and Ezekiel (Sir 49:8).

The role of Micah in the Twelve has factored into discussions about how the twelve writings came together because a number of studies include Micah as one of four prophetic collections brought into conversation at an early stage when they were copied together onto a scroll that has been called the Book of the Four in recent years.52 Even without resorting to detailed redactional analysis, however, the sequence of Hosea, Amos, Micah, and Zephaniah can hardly be accidental. They always appear in the same order relative to one another even when one factors in the Septuagint order, where Hosea, Amos, and Micah (the three eighth-century prophets mentioning kings of Judah and Israel) begin the Twelve. The structure of the four individual books, when combined, creates a sequence with a theological pattern. The logic of this pattern appears in terms of geography and message. Geographically, the speeches recorded in Hosea and Amos deal primarily with problems of the Northern Kingdom, though both books also (briefly) incorporate warnings to Judah as well. By contrast, in the speeches of Micah and Zephaniah, the people of Judah in Jerusalem function as the primary audience. Micah mentions Samaria in the superscription and the opening speech (1:1, 5), but Samaria has already been destroyed, and its destruction serves as a warning to Jerusalem and Judah about the fate that awaits them if they do not change. Unlike Hosea and Amos, Micah does not address prophetic oracles to the Northern Kingdom because it has already been destroyed.

These four books, based especially upon their thematic structure, also exhibit parallel messages that represent theological decisions and overlap with the geographic orientation. Given that these four books contain two books focused upon the Northern Kingdom and two books that focus on the Southern Kingdom, interpreters should not miss the fact that the first book of each group (Hosea and Micah) structures its threats by alternating pronouncements of judgment with word of hope and deliverance multiple times. Hosea and Micah thus confront their respective audiences with the need to change their behavior, while at the same time conveying the message that such change can influence Yahweh’s decision to destroy the respective kingdoms of Israel in Hosea and Judah in Micah. By contrast, both Amos and Zephaniah assume from the very beginning that Yahweh has made the decision to punish Israel and Judah. Amos contains no explicit word of hope that Israel can avoid Yahweh’s wrath. The only words of “hope” appear at the end of the book, but the two speeches therein deal with the possibility of a remnant surviving. The first (9:7–10) hints at the possibility that a remnant may survive “among all the nations” after being scattered (9:10). The second speech (9:11–15) devotes more space to life after judgment. To be sure it speaks of restoring “the fortunes of my people Israel,” but these verses describe the remnant’s main purpose as rebuilding ruined cities (9:14), a promise that is tinged with memories of failure. This promise only makes sense once the kingdom has been destroyed. Relatedly, like several texts in Hosea, this promise assumes that the surviving people will be ruled by a descendant of David.53 Israel, then, will not return as an independent kingdom, but will become part of Judah after it has also been overthrown.54

The role of Micah as linchpin (discussed above) can be seen in the means by which Mic 1:2–7 utilizes the destruction of Samaria as a warning to Jerusalem and Judah, explicitly in 1:5 and implicitly in 1:9, 12, 13 with the references to the “gate of my people.” Yahweh’s prophets warned Israel, the Northern Kingdom, in Hosea and Amos, but they did not listen. The same dynamic appears with the message of Micah and Zephaniah, except that the subject changes to the sins of Judah and Jerusalem. Additionally, Mic 1:2–7, 9, 12, 13 manifest additional reminders that Yahweh expects obedience by drawing upon knowledge of the destruction of the Northern Kingdom.

Finally, one should not overlook Micah’s role in the Twelve as it relates to the treatment of the fate of the nations. As already noted, Assyria (and Babylon to a lesser degree) surface in Micah as empires that play a role in the punishment of Judah and Jerusalem, as well as Israel and Samaria. Micah also presupposes a future point in time when Yahweh will also punish foreign nations (4:3, 12–13) and make Zion the (purified) center of the known world (Mic 4:1–4). The fact that this passage repeats Isa 2:2–4, essentially verbatim, and that Mic 4:1 represents the first verse of the second half of the Twelve certainly suggests the importance of these verses for the final form of the Twelve and the entire prophetic corpus.55 The passage in Micah, when read as the midpoint of the Twelve, reminds readers that Yahweh’s punishment of Judah, Israel, and the nations does not mean that Yahweh is a capricious God, though the Twelve repeatedly presents Yahweh as a jealous god who intends to hold Israel and Judah accountable for breaking their promise to live in accordance with Yahweh’s expectations. Words of hope often articulate what that purpose looks like. Judgment speeches in Micah and the Twelve point to a grander purpose for that judgment. In the Twelve, Yahweh mixes words of judgment with words of hope and purpose for all humanity. Micah does the same. In both Micah and the Twelve, Yahweh’s relationship with Israel and Judah is perceived as distinct from his relationship with the nations. Neither Micah nor the Twelve, however, convey a theology that considers foreigners to be evil simply because they are foreign. They are judged for their attitudes and actions toward Yahweh, including how they treat Judah and Israel.





VI. CONTEMPLATING MICAH TODAY


How does one proceed to evaluate the significance of Micah for communities of faith today? Several issues come into play to answer this question. One of the most important issues concerns the starting point for interpreting Old Testament texts. First, context matters. This statement means that one should deliberate over the question and, to the best of one’s ability, consider the historical, literary, and theological context of Micah on its own terms before turning to the question of application. Of course, there will always be time constraints for such study, but the art of interpretation does not give the interpreter carte blanche to make the text say something that it does not. Interpreting Micah for Christian communities of faith does not imply that we seek to understand the book as a work of Christian theology or that we assume the authors of these texts first wrote the words to Christian audiences. Interpreters should understand that the book of Micah arose in pre-Christian times and in Jewish contexts. Two passages will illustrate how this might play out: Mic 6:6–8 and 5:1–3 (4:14–5:2).

Micah 6:6–8 has a very different historical and religious context than the religious world of today. The author wrote these verses at a time when the religious practices of the audience included the literal sacrifice of animals. The author formulates this speech to make a rhetorical point that challenges the idea that Yahweh needs the blood of the sacrifice for Yahweh’s own benefit. It appears as part of a larger unit that presents itself as a trial speech.

Relatedly, one must recognize that 6:6–8 assumes two speakers. In 6:6–7 the first-person verbs and pronouns must be seen as the words of Yahweh’s opponent who interrupts Yahweh’s speech from the preceding verses (where the first-person verbs require Yahweh as the subject). Micah 6:6–7 also speak of Yahweh in the third person, solidifying the assumption that Yahweh is not speaking. With considerable rhetorical flourish, the speaker seeks to prove his innocence. In 6:6, the first-person speaker begins to challenge the need to offer sacrifice to Yahweh, essentially asking how much blood Yahweh requires to be appeased. By contrast, 6:8 addresses a human (ʾādām) and offers a rejoinder to the hyperbolic formulation 6:6–7. Nevertheless, this speaker also talks about Yahweh in the third person. Consequently, understanding 6:6–8 requires the interpreter to conceptualize these verses as a confrontational dialogue in which Yahweh’s opponent interrupts Yahweh’s preceding speech and contests the idea that the speaker has done anything wrong. The response to this interruption in 6:8 comes from the prophet, not Yahweh, and the prophet admonishes the opponent with a powerful statement of his own that will not allow the opponent to claim innocence. Ironically, the prophet’s response in 6:8 basically accepts the opponent’s claim that Yahweh does not need blood sacrifice, but that the opponent has ignored a deeper guilt that does not involve sacrifice: he has failed “to do justice, to love kindness [ḥesed], and to walk modestly with … God.” In a further irony for the contemporary person of faith, Judaism and Christianity later rejected animal sacrifice as a necessary component for worship.

Just as significantly, the beginning of 6:8 begins the prophet’s response by telling the opponent that he has already been told to do these things (do justice, love ḥesed, walk with God). Yet, when (or where) was he told what is good and what God expects? These terms are not typical for Micah. These words appear more frequently in Hosea and in Amos than in Micah. “Justice” (mišpāṭ) does appear elsewhere in Micah but in the sense of “executing judgment” rather than justice (3:1, 8–9; 7:9). “Justice,” however, appears more frequently in Hosea and Amos (Hos 2:21; 5:1, 11; 6:5; 10:4; 12:7; Amos 5:7, 15, 24; 6:12). The verb “love” appears only one other place in Micah (3:2), but appears some nineteen times in Hosea (2:7, 9, 12, 14–15; 3:1 [four times]; 4:18 [twice]; 8:9; 9:1, 10, 15; 10:11; 11:1; 12:6; and 14:5) The only other place where the verb “love” appears in Micah, it appears as part of an accusation of wrongdoing. There, in Mic 3:2, the prophet blames rulers for “hating good and loving evil,” precisely the opposite of what Mic 6:8 indicates the man has been told. The Hebrew word ḥesed appears twice more in Micah, but not until chapter 7. If one is reading Micah sequentially, the statement in 6:8 precedes 7:18, 20, so on a literary level the man has not yet been told anything about ḥesed. One can make a case that the phrase to “walk with God” could point to Mic 4:2, 5 since the verb “walk” and the noun ʾelôhîm (“god” or “gods”) appear together, albeit with a different preposition. One verse in Hosea comes very close, however, to expressing these three commands: “But as for you, return to your God, hold fast to love and justice, and wait continually for your God” (Hos 12:6).
