In a certain sense, then, one could say that the prophet’s admonition requires texts from Hosea, Amos, and Micah to explain the statement in Mic 6:8, so if one assumes that Micah expects its readers to know Hosea and Amos, then the accusation in Micah takes on more meaning.

The second text, Mic 5:1–3 (4:14–5:2), serves as a warning against superimposing an overtly Christian interpretation onto Micah. Of course, New Testament writers do precisely this when they interpret Mic 5:2 as a christological prediction for the birth of the messiah, though to be precise, these formulations diverge slightly from the wording in Micah, and each writer puts the words in a different context: in the mouths of the magi addressing Herod (Matt 2:5–6), when the shepherds speak to one another after their visit from the angels (Luke 2:15), and in the confessions among some in the crowd who heard Jesus speak shortly before his arrest (John 7:40–42). In other words, two of these references take place in the birth narratives of their respective gospel, while the third recounts it as a climactic statement foreshadowing the end of Jesus’s earthly ministry. Truly, the gospel writers use Mic 5:2 to affirm Jesus came as Messiah. This statement is not the same, however, as saying that we should interpret the original intention of Mic 5:2 as a messianic prediction of Jesus. In its Old Testament context, Mic 5:1–3 concerns Yahweh’s use of a descendant of David to save Jerusalem from a siege and to bring back those taken into exile. The beginning of the interpretive process takes the Old Testament context as foundational. One can, however, still ask how the theological message of Micah has relevance for modern communities of faith without resorting to an anachronistic reading.

A theological reading as described above entails several things simultaneously. It includes a historically informed exegetical process that remains true to the intent of the biblical text, as best we can understand it. In the case of Micah, one can read the text against the historical and sociological backdrop of Judah in the eighth century and in the aftermath of the destruction of Jerusalem. Such readings contextualize the message of the book and convey a story. One can also read Micah in light of the theological themes it conveys and look for contemporary parallels. Finding contemporary parallels should, however, avoid conveying the idea that these points of connection represent the one true meaning of the text. Texts, including biblical texts, derive meaning from the interplay of the words authors use, the reasons for writing the text in this specific fashion, the presuppositions of ancient and contemporary readers, and the venue in which the audience receives that interpretation. This commentary is not a sermon, but drawing upon a commentary may help one write a better sermon. A sermon is not the same as a Bible study in a college dorm, and a Bible study is not the same as an exegetical paper written for a seminary class. One adapts one’s interpretation to the context. One cannot, however, forget that the book of Micah was written in Hebrew, and that knowledge obligates interpreters to take seriously the fact that they are primarily reading Micah in English. The adage that something is lost in translation is certainly true when interpreting a biblical text like Micah.

Hopefully, this and other commentaries will help readers consider the nuances of Hebrew words, phrases, and idioms. Individual Hebrew words, for example, can mean different things in different contexts. For example, the Hebrew word mišpaṭ can mean “justice” or “judgment,” but it can also imply both. When we admonish one another “to strive for justice in the world,” we do not mean the same thing when we say that a judge “will mete out justice” when someone is found guilty of a crime. The former intends a desire for equity, while the latter implies punishment. The verb one selects creates different understandings. These two uses of the same word have more in common, however, than might be apparent at first glance. They both assume that human beings should act responsibly and should be held accountable in this world.

Relatedly, phrases like dəbar yəhwāh (“the word of Yahweh”) or bayôm hahûʾ (“on that day”) express more than what a literal translation means in English. The phrase dəbar yəhwāh conveys the idea that Yahweh has communicated to and through a prophetic figure. At the same time, it conveys a divine imprimatur on the speech that follows. Prophets do not speak or write under their own authority when they claim to speak for Yahweh. This conviction holds true for the prophets who delivered the message originally, for those who recorded the words for the first time, and for the scribal prophets who expanded the book of Micah over the following centuries. Uttering the word of Yahweh carries great responsibility.

The phrase bayôm hahûʾ in a prophetic speech conveys eschatological overtones. In a prophetic book, it almost always introduces a unit that relates to a future point in time when the following situation will be realized (generally, the more distant future). At the same time, the phrase does not generally specify an exact date and time. By contrast, this phrase also appears more than three dozen times in Old Testament narrative literature, but in those instances “on that day” refers to specific events in the past. Both tendencies are driven by the genre expectations of a given text. Biblical narratives tell stories about figures from the past within a theological framework, and the phrase “on that day” generally refers to a specific point within the narrative context. In essence, the relative pronoun “that” assumes an antecedent from the literary context, but the antecedent functions proleptically in prophetic literature.

Recurring themes also appear in Micah, most notably the implications of fidelity to Yahweh for Yahweh’s people, challenging the abuse of power, and the juxtaposition of judgment and hope. These themes often resonate with modern parallels, though details will change. We do not live in a society where we are beholden to the arbitrary whims of a king, but most of us still have authority figures who hold us accountable. Translating the theme of fidelity to Yahweh into modern settings recognizes that Micah assumes Yahweh is the king by whom Yahweh’s people will ultimately be judged. Christians do not get a free pass to act as they wish merely because their faith in Christ gives them hope that they will be redeemed. Ephesians 1:11–12 makes it abundantly clear that faith calls us to “live for the praise of his glory.”

Old Testament prophets speaking under the authority of Yahweh take on the powerful, confronting kings, princes, priests, government officials, and foreign occupiers. Ordinary people would not dare to speak as blatantly as the Old Testament prophets do. Even prophets were not immune to punishment or death, but they understood the command from Yahweh to prophesy as superseding any threats from those in power.56 Micah’s judgment speeches take the people of Judah to task for wrongs they have committed. These speeches condemn idolatry in chapter 1. Micah then takes on the elite of Judah (see 3:1) for taking property to which they were not entitled throughout chapters 2–3. Prophets do not appear as timid persons of faith when it comes to challenging social inequity or violence. Modern interpreters of Micah should not ignore problems in our time and in our own communities. We should not ignore the fact that the book of Micah confronts issues of another time and place. Rather, it should challenge us to do the same. In our society, issues such as systemic racism, income inequity, excessive violence, and spewing hatred on social media platforms deserve to be countered. The book of Micah encourages us to speak up against injustice and violence. It calls us to live up to the ideals of justice, kindness, and humility. We may not use the same literary forms (esp. formulaic judgment speeches, for example), but Micah provides a powerful model to speak about changing behavior and challenging injustice.

How one approaches the juxtaposition of hope and judgment has implications for the interpretive process. One should recognize that most people in modern communities of faith fear reading Old Testament prophetic texts because so many of these texts portray Yahweh as a God of wrath. Judgment predominates in these texts to be sure, but it should not blind us to the message of hope that appears in all four prophetic scrolls (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the Twelve). Most prophetic books end with words of hope. The book of Micah is no different. Chapters 1–3 contain only two verses of hope (2:12–13), but even those words are not always interpreted as hopeful.57 Hope plays a much larger role in chapters 4–7.58 Significantly, the Masoretes marked Mic 4:1 as the precise middle of the Twelve by verses, and it begins a passage (4:1–4) that is arguably the most hopeful passage in Micah and the Twelve. It also repeats Isa 2:2–4, thus joining the first and last of the four prophetic scrolls in the Hebrew canon through expressions of hope, not judgment. One should not underestimate the fact that Mic 4:1 begins the second half of the Book of the Twelve by offering a powerful message of Yahweh’s hopeful purpose for Jerusalem, Judah, and the nations.

Thus, a message of hope carries significant weight in Micah, as well as in the Book of the Twelve as a whole, even though more space is devoted to judgment than to hope. Learning to incorporate this message into our interpretive processes opens productive avenues for applying prophetic texts to modern communities of faith, but it also testifies to the message of the books as they were shaped theologically. Choosing to emphasize hope is not contrary to the message that the book of Micah expects us to hear.

The book of Sirach certainly recognizes this hermeneutical truth for the entire Twelve. Sirach 49:10 characterizes the Twelve prophets as a book of hope, despite the fact that more of its verses confront Yahweh’s people with words of judgment and warning. We can make productive use of Micah by following the lead of Sirach: “May the bones of the Twelve Prophets send forth new life from where they lie, for they comforted the people of Jacob and delivered them with confident hope” (NRSV). May they provide us with the same.





VII. ANALYSIS OF CONTENTS


I.Judgment on Samaria and Jerusalem (1:1–16)

A.Superscription (1:1)

B.Yahweh Comes for Judgment (1:2–7)

1.Theophany Report against the Nations (1:2)

2.Theophany Description (1:3–4)

3.Threat against Judah after Samaria’s Destruction (1:5–7)

C.The Prophet Laments and Calls the Shephelah to Do the Same (1:8–16)

1.The Prophet’s Own Lament (1:8–9)

2.Warning to the Shephelah and Jerusalem (1:10–16)

II.Greed, Evil, Confrontation, and Hope (2:1–13)

A.Woe to the Strong Oppressing the Weak (2:1–5)

B.A Prophet Disputing His Enemies (2:6–11)

C.Hope beyond Judgment (2:12–13)

III.Judgment on Jerusalem’s Leadership (3:1–12)

A.Justice for Leaders Devouring Their Own (3:1–4)

B.Justice for False Prophets: They Will Not Speak (3:5–8)

C.Leadership Causes Jerusalem’s Destruction (3:9–12)

IV.The Future for Judah and the Nations (4:1–5:15[14])

A.Eschatological Day Sayings (4:1–7)

1.Peace at the End of the Days (4:1–5)

2.Gathering the Remnant on That Day (4:6–7)

B.You and Now (4:8–5:4[3])

1.“You” Will See the Former Dominion (4:8)

2.“Now,” Why Do You Shout? (4:9–10)

3.“Now” the Nations Will Be Punished (4:11–13)

4.“Now,” Nations Gather against You (5:1 [4:14])

5.“You” Will See a New Ruler (5:2–4[1–3])

C.And It Will Be (5:4–9[4–8])

D.On That Day I Will Cut Off (5:10–15[9–14])

V.Lawsuit, Verdict, and Hope (6:1–7:20)

A.Speech of the Prosecutor (6:1–5)

B.The Defendant’s Interruption (6:6–8)

C.The Charges and the Verdict (6:9–16)

D.The Prophet’s Lament (7:1–7)

E.Zion’s Affirmation and Yahweh’s Promise (7:8–20)

1.Lady Zion Addresses Lady Nineveh (7:8–10)

2.The Prophet Addresses Lady Zion about Reprieve and Punishment (7:11–13)

3.The Prophet’s Intercession and Yahweh’s Response (7:14–15)

4.The People Respond to Yahweh (7:16–17)

5.The People’s Hymn about Yahweh (7:18–20)





1. See more extensive discussion below on the unity of Micah. Here, discussion of two very different commentaries will illustrate that this statement has a long and deep history in scholarly research, even though no consensus exists on the precise dating of the later materials. In their history of research, Andersen and Freedman are not quick to jettison the idea that Micah wrote or spoke significant portions of the book, but even they admit one cannot place the entirety of the book in the eighth century BCE. Frances I. Andersen and David Noel Freedman, Micah: A New Translation with Introduction and Commentary, AB 24E (New York: Doubleday, 2000), 17–20. Even though they express skepticism about precise datings, they admit the book’s final form may have been edited in the time of Ezra, in the middle of the fifth century, though on the same page they indicate their preference that Micah was revised before the Persian period. They apparently distinguish between revisions and editorial work. Notably, Utzschneider begins his commentary by treating Micah as a dramatic text that unfolds in two acts (chs. 1–5 and 6–7). Helmut Utzschneider, Micha, ZBK 24.1 (Zurich: TVZ, 2005), 11–16. He writes extensively about distinguishing the portrait of the prophetic figure in the book from what one can say about the historical person from the eighth century (21–25). Rather than attempting a redaction history as such, Utzschneider offers a series of “observations” that demonstrate his recognition of the composite nature of the texts (25–29). E.g., these observations lead him to conclude that 2:6–12 stems from the time of Jeremiah. Utzschneider concludes that 4:1–5 comes from the Hellenistic period (332–67 BCE) and that 6:9–16 and 7:1–7 are best understood against the backdrop of the Persian period (538–332 BCE), but most likely in the fifth to fourth centuries BCE.

2. The date when Hezekiah took the throne remains notoriously difficult to determine, but it is most commonly considered to be around 725 BCE. The reasons for the difficulty include a possible period as coregent, contradictory dates for the death of Hezekiah’s father, Ahaz, and incompatible sources. Some, therefore, deduce that his reign begins in 715 BCE. E.g., see notes regarding the problems in Hugh B. MacLean, “Ahaz,” IDB 1:64; Gösta W. Ahlström, The History of Ancient Palestine (Minneapolis: Fortress, 1993), 689–91; Jonathan Rosenbaum, “Hezekiah, King of Judah,” ABD 3:189–90.

3. E.g., see Reinhard Gregor Kratz, Historisches und biblisches Israel: Drei Überblicke zum Alten Testament (Tübingen: Mohr Siebeck, 2013), 32; Gary N. Knoppers, Jews and Samaritans: The Origins and History of Their Early Relations (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2013), 24–25, 80–87.

4. See Norman K. Gottwald, The Politics of Ancient Israel, LAI (Louisville: Westminster John Knox, 2001), 68–69; Sandra Richter, “Eighth-Century Issues: The World of Jeroboam II, the Fall of Samaria, and the Reign of Hezekiah,” in Ancient Israel’s History: An Introduction to Issues and Sources, ed. Bill T. Arnold and Richard S. Hess (Grand Rapids: Baker Academic, 2014), 319–49. See the monograph of Young, and especially the summary of Hezekiah’s contributions. Robb Andrew Young, Hezekiah in History and Tradition, VTSup 155 (Leiden: Brill, 2012), 285–88, 293.

5. See the discussion of the editorial activity in these verses in the commentary on Mic 1.

6. See Leslie J. Hoppe, “Sennacherib Invades Syro-Palestine,” in Great Events from History: The Ancient World, Prehistory–476 C.E., ed. Mark W. Chavalas, 2 vols. (Pasadena, CA: Salem, 2004), 1:314–16; and the monograph by William R. Gallagher, Sennacherib’s Campaign to Judah: New Studies, SHCANE 18 (Leiden: Brill, 1999). The differences in the accounts have led a few scholars to postulate Sennacherib invaded twice. See, e.g., John Bright, A History of Israel, 2nd ed. (Philadelphia: Westminster, 1972), 282–56, 296–308. Few follow this path. See the alternative discussion that focuses upon the ideological purposes of the authors of the various accounts in Mordechai Cogan, “Cross-Examining the Assyrian Witnesses to Sennacherib’s Third Campaign: Assessing the Limits of Historical Reconstruction,” in Sennacherib at the Gates of Jerusalem: Story, History, and Historiography, ed. Isaac Kalimi and Seth Richardson, CHANE 71 (Leiden: Brill, 2014), 51–74. See especially his analysis of the unlikely prospects of a second campaign (73–74).

7. For English translations of Sennacherib’s account, see A. Leo Oppenheim, “Sennacherib,” ANET, 287–88; and “Sennacherib’s Siege of Jerusalem,” trans. Mordechai Cogan, COS 2.119B:302–3.

8. Reading these accounts in parallel to one another quickly shows both the similarities and the differences. See James D. Newsome Jr., ed., A Synoptic Harmony of Samuel, Kings, and Chronicles with Related Passages from Psalms, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezra (Grand Rapids: Baker, 1986), 217–41.

9. The Sennacherib account appears in three nearly identical prisms. One is held by the Israel Museum in Jerusalem and is dated within a few months of the events in 700 BCE (“Sennacherib’s Siege,” COS 2.119B:302). A second copy called the Taylor prism was produced in 691 BCE and is now housed in the British Museum in London. The third copy, called the Chicago prism, dates to 691 BCE and is in the Institute for the Study of Ancient Civilizations in Chicago. Additionally, the British Museum has fragments of other copies.

10. The writer of Chronicles adds an entire story detailing how Manasseh was taken prisoner to Babylon by the army of Assyria (2 Chr 33:11–17, 19). In this account, while a prisoner in Babylon, Manasseh experiences a dramatic change of heart. He prays to Yahweh who allows Manasseh to return to Jerusalem as king. As a result, Manasseh reverses course and institutes a series of religious reforms designed to purify the cult and lead the people to worship Yahweh.

11. Scholars typically consider this Book of the Law to be an early version of the book of Deuteronomy. See Rainer Albertz, A History of Israelite Religion in the Old Testament Period, vol. 1: From the Beginnings to the End of the Monarchy, trans. John Bowden, OTL (Louisville: Westminster John Knox, 1994), 198–206; Ahlström, History of Ancient Palestine, 454–61; J. Maxwell Miller and John H. Hayes, A History of Ancient Israel and Judah, 2nd ed. (Louisville: Westminster John Knox, 2006), 763–65, 770–81.

12. Albertz, History of Israelite Religion, 1:201–6.

13. Debates continue regarding precise timing and locations of Nebuchadnezzar’s incursions into Syria-Palestine, but he claims to have conducted military expeditions into Syria-Palestine (Hatti land). The Babylonian Chronicles specify that he remained in Babylon his fifth year during which he refurbished and enlarged his chariot army, but they do not specify what he did in the other two years. See “The Conquest of Jerusalem,” ANET, 564; and Bill T. Arnold, “The Neo-Babylonian Chronicle Series,” in The Ancient Near East: Historical Sources in Translation, ed. Mark W. Chavalas, Blackwell Sourcebooks in Ancient History (Oxford: Blackwell, 2006), 407–26; see esp. Chronicle 5, pp. 416–17. This refurbishment followed a battle with Egypt in his fourth year that took a heavy toll on his military capabilities. Note that the two translations differ with regard to what Nebuchadnezzar did in year 5. The former says the king “organized his chariots and many horses,” while the latter indicates that the king “gathered a great many chariots and horses.” At any rate, in year 6, Nebuchadnezzar raided Arab tribes with considerable economic benefit. In year 7 Nebuchadnezzar laid siege to Jerusalem, and after he took it, “he appointed a (new) king to his liking.” He does not specify that he took Jehoiachin prisoner, but his claim to have replaced the king corresponds to the time of the appointment of Zedekiah.

14. This date is unusually precisely stated and is seen as evidence that it generated a hope for the return of Davidic kingship since this account of his change in status (2 Kgs 25:27–30; Jer 52:31–34) concludes both the book of Kings and Jeremiah. Jehoiachin’s elevation that allowed him to dine daily at the king’s table occurred in his thirty-seventh year in exile according to 2 Kgs 25:27 and Jer 52:31. Jehoiachin was deported in the first wave in 597. By contrast, the Chronicler omits this account entirely and replaces it with the opening verses of the book of Ezra. Cf. Ezra 1:1–4 and 2 Chr 36:22–23.

15. After Zedekiah fled Jerusalem in the dead of night, the Babylonian army captured him and took him north to Riblah (roughly two hundred miles from Jerusalem) where Nebuchadnezzar’s army had gone. The Babylonian king then slaughtered Zedekiah’s sons in front of Zedekiah. He then poked out his eyes, so that the death of his sons would be the last thing he saw. The Babylonians then bound him in fetters and forced him to march to Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar intended these brutal acts as a warning against any further rebellion.

16. See Albertz, History of Israelite Religion, 1:241–42. Albertz highlights the partisan battle between the nationalists loyal to the king and the reformers who sought social change. Gedaliah belonged to the reformers. He sought the redistribution of property ownership as potentially the foundation for major change in the economic structure. He placed the population without land on the large estates that had been abandoned following the exile of their owners. Gedaliah’s reforms coalesced closely with the social harmony and balance that Deuteronomy articulates.

17. A brief story of Gedaliah appears in 2 Kgs 25:22–26, but an expanded version appears in Jer 40:5–41:3. The Jeremiah account portrays Gedaliah most positively. It details Gedaliah’s actions to grow crops to feed the country, which included appointing the poorest of the land who remained in Judah to run the farms (Jer 40:7), as well as his intentions to bring Judeans living in Moab, Ammon, Edom, and elsewhere to have enough people to work the farms (40:10–11). Jeremiah’s account also stresses the great abundance of food that came from Gedaliah’s efforts (40:12).

18. In this respect, the prophetic figure functions in similar ways to the prophet in Isa 40–66. Seitz explores this idea in terms of the portrait of the prophetic figure, and Steck speaks in similar terms concerning the metahistorical perspective of the prophetic book structured as God walking through history. See Christopher R. Seitz, “How Is the Prophet Isaiah Present in the Latter Half of the Book? The Logic of Chapters 40–66 within the Book of Isaiah,” JBL 115 (1996): 219–40, DOI: 10.2307/3266853; Odil Hannes Steck, The Theological Witness of Prophetic Books, trans. James D. Nogalski (St. Louis: Chalice, 2000), 3–114, esp. 9–13, 48–52, 114; for Jeremiah, see Konrad Schmid, Buchgestalten des Jeremiabuches: Untersuchungen zur Redaktions- und Rezeptionsgeschichte von Jer 30–33 im Kontext des Buches, WMANT 72 (Neukirchen-Vluyn: Neukirchener, 1996), 229–49; and for Micah, see James D. Nogalski, Introduction to the Hebrew Prophets (Nashville: Abingdon, 2018), 128–29.

19. The vast majority of scholars assume that Mic 1–3 derive from prophetic material attributed to the prophet Micah, but that some portions may reflect later editorial activity, including at least portions of 1:1, 5–7, 9, 12, 13; and 2:12–13. Discussion of these claims will be noted in the commentary. A few scholars date passages that appear in portions of Mic 4–7 as arising in the eighth century, and a few scholars have opted to assign virtually the entire book to the eighth century. Nevertheless, there remains a significant pattern of recognizing the three parts of Micah (chs. 1–3, 4–5, and 6–7) and acknowledging that they have a complicated history. At the same time, more commentators are reluctant to speculate about the details. See the discussions in Daniel L. Smith-Christopher, Micah: A Commentary, OTL (Louisville: Westminster John Knox, 2015), 32–42. He prefers to speak in terms of the coherence of these parts and their relationship to the book as a whole. Andersen and Freedman rehearse previous research on Micah, but while they recognize that Mic 4–7 took its final shape after Jerusalem’s destruction, they do not present their own theory of the process by which these chapters were added and are skeptical of those who do (Andersen and Freedman, 27–37). They imply that Mic 6–7 entered after chs. 4–5, but they believe the book of Micah was completed in the early part of the Persian period at the latest.

20. Aaron Schart, Die Entstehung des Zwölfprophetenbuchs: Neubearbeitungen von Amos im Rahmen schriftenuebergreifender Redaktionsprozesse, BZAW 250 (Berlin: de Gruyter, 1998), 178–79; James D. Nogalski, Literary Precursors of the Book of the Twelve, BZAW 217 (Berlin: de Gruyter, 1993), 133–34. These dates are, of course, debated. One does find scholars who treat these chapters earlier and later. E.g., Utzschneider, *25–27. He believes that the first act of the drama contains an earliest form of the book that ran from 1:10–5:3 prior to the addition of the Zion material in 4:1–7. He notes, however, that certain word sequences and passages may go back to the eighth century. By contrast, he believes Mic 4:1–5 stems from the Hellenistic period. See also Andersen and Freedman, 11. They straddle the fence by acknowledging the scholarly consensus that dates these chapters to the exilic or postexilic period, but they see the references to Assyria as “realistic,” and the reference to Judah’s exile to Babylon is “quite general.” They then coyly state that their “minds are also open to the possibility that Babylon was part of the prophets’ world map even in the eighth century.”

21. The formulas include the phrases: And it will happen in the end of days (4:1); And on that day (4:6; 5:10). These formulas appear at the beginning of the first two units (4:1–5, 6–7) and the last unit in these chapters (5:10–15).

22. Micah 1:1 does not date the beginning of Micah’s prophetic activity until the time of Ahaz, while Isa 1:1 places Isaiah’s appearance during the reigns of the Judean kings Uzziah (786–746 BCE), Jotham (756–741 BCE), Ahaz (742–725 BCE), and Hezekiah (725–696 BCE). Yet, Isa 40–66 has long been considered to contain late exilic and postexilic additions to a core collection from the eighth century (and many argue a significant update from the time of Josiah in the last decades of the seventh century). There is little doubt about the Persian period setting of chs. 40–55 since Cyrus, king of Persia (559–530 BCE) is mentioned by name in Isa 44:28; 45:1. These verses presuppose a time after 539 BCE when Cyrus granted permission for exiles in Babylon to return to Jerusalem. Isaiah 56–66 come later since they presuppose the existence of the restored temple.

23. The term Book of the Twelve refers to the prophetic corpus that already by 200 BCE contained the twelve prophetic books of Hosea–Malachi on a single scroll. This collection is also commonly called “the Twelve,” “the Twelve Prophets,” and “the Minor Prophets.” For a more extensive discussion of this scroll, and the implications of counting it as one book, not twelve, see James D. Nogalski, Joel, Obadiah, and Jonah, NICOT (Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 2023), 1–12; and Nogalski, Introduction to the Hebrew Prophets, 97–102. An abbreviated summary of this material as it relates to textual transmission appears below when discussing the textual transmission of Micah and how to read Micah within the Twelve.

24. Fishbane documented the phenomenon of innerbiblical interpretation that relied upon extensive knowledge of biblical texts. Michael Fishbane, Biblical Interpretation in Ancient Israel (Oxford: Clarendon, 1985). From there, several important studies have explored the nature of scribal education and its effect upon the canon of the Hebrew Bible. See esp. David M. Carr, Writing on the Tablet of the Heart: Origins of Scripture and Literature (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2005); Karel van der Toorn, Scribal Culture and the Making of the Hebrew Bible (Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 2007); Martti Nissinen, Ancient Prophecy: Near Eastern, Biblical, and Greek Perspectives (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2017).

25. See James D. Nogalski, “How Does Malachi’s Book of Remembrance Function for the Cultic Elite?,” in Priests and Cults in the Book of the Twelve, ed. Lena-Sofia Tiemeyer, ANEM 14 (Atlanta: SBL Press, 2016), 191–212, esp. 201–3.

26. See James D. Nogalski, “Recurring Themes in the Book of the Twelve: Creating Points of Contact for a Theological Reading,” Int 61 (2007): 125–36, DOI: 10.1177/00209643070610020.

27. The Twelve Prophets were copied on a single scroll and counted as a single book, pairing the four scrolls of the Latter Prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the Twelve) with the scrolls of the four Former Prophets (Joshua, Judges, Samuel, and Kings). See n. 23 above and the discussion of “the Twelve” below in the section titled “Reading Micah in the Twelve.”

28. See the discussion in Nogalski, Introduction to the Hebrew Prophets, xvi–xx, 128–29; Odil Hannes Steck, Der Abschluβ der Prophetie im Alten Testament: Ein Versuch zur Frage der Vorgeschichte des Kanons, BThSt 17 (Neukirchen-Vluyn: Neukirchener, 1991), 11–24.

29.Andersen and Freedman, 110; James L. Mays, Micah: A Commentary, OTL (Philadelphia: Westminster, 1976), 59; Smith-Christopher, 15–16; Marvin A. Sweeney, The Twelve Prophets, vol. 2: Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi, Berit Olam (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2000), 344; Ralph Smith, Micah–Malachi, WBC 32 (Waco, TX: Word, 1984), 14. See the map provided by Jörg Jeremias, Die Propheten Joel, Obadja, Jona, Micha, ATD 24.3 (Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 2007), 142.

30. In addition to recounting the narrative of Jeroboam’s decision to establish these two places of sacrifice for fear the people of Israel would return to worship at Jerusalem, Jeroboam also set up two golden calves and offered sacrifice at Bethel (1 Kgs 12:26–33). Moreover, the author of Kings continues to condemn all the kings of Israel (as well as some Judean kings) for continuing to follow the “sin(s) of Jeroboam” (1 Kgs 13:34; 14:16; 15:30, 34; 16:2, 19, 26, 31; 21:22; 22:52; 2 Kgs 3:3; 10:29, 31; 13:2, 6, 11; 14:24; 15:9, 18, 24, 28; 17:21–22; 23:15). This leitmotif thus becomes the code by which the author reminds the readers that the Northern Kingdom was founded upon rebellion.

31. “Sennacherib (704–681),” ANET, 288; “Sennacherib’s Siege of Jerusalem,” COS 2.119B:303.

32. A similar adaptation of a place-name also occurs in the Greek version of Amos 9:11. See James D. Nogalski, “The Problematic Suffixes of Amos 9:11,” VT 43 (1993): 411–18.

33. The majority of scholars continue to follow the view of Ziegler that a single translator is responsible for the Septuagint translation of the Twelve, though the recensions of the Greek translations are quite complex. Joseph Ziegler, ed., Duodecim Prophetae, 3rd ed., SVTG 13 (Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 1984), 119–40.

34. See the very helpful synopsis of the text of the extant Hebrew and Greek texts in Beate Ego et al., eds., Biblia Qumranica, vol. 3B: Minor Prophets (Leiden: Brill, 2005), 90–111. These Hebrew texts include 1Q14, 4Q168, 4Q82, and Mur 88. In addition to the Septuagint, a Greek manuscript of Micah has also been found (8Ḥev 1). A critical edition of the Septuagint has been consulted for this commentary: Ziegler, Duodecim Prophetae.

35. Thus, 4Q82 is dated to the last third of the first century BCE and contains verses from Hosea–Zechariah, and Mur 88 contains portions of Joel–Zechariah. 4Q76 contains portions of Jonah, Zechariah, and Malachi. 4Q77 contains portions of Zephaniah and Haggai, including the last verses of Zephaniah and the initial verses of Haggai. 4Q78 does not contain verses from Micah, but contains parts of Hosea, Joel, Amos, Zephaniah, and Malachi. 8Ḥev 1 (a Greek manuscript also known as the Nahal Hever manuscript) is missing the beginning of the scroll, but contains portions of Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, and Zechariah. It is dated to the last quarter of the first century BCE. 4Q80 contains parts of Haggai and Zechariah. 4Q81 contains parts of Jonah 1 and Mic 5:2–3, and is deemed one of the older manuscripts (175–50 BCE). 4Q79 only contains a portion of Hos 1–2.

36. Only Mic 5:4 does not appear in some portion of one of the early Hebrew manuscripts. This verse does appear, however, in 8Ḥev 1, a manuscript typically dated to the first century CE.

37. Portions of the following twenty-seven verses appear in 8Ḥev 1: 1:1–8; 2:7–8; 3:4–6; 4:3–10; and 5:1–6. This list represents only slightly more than 25 percent of the 105 verses in Micah, but since not every verse in the list is complete, the number of words represents an even smaller percentage of the text of Micah. E.g., Mic 4:10 in 8Ḥev 1 has only three Greek words while MT has twenty-one Hebrew words. This small percentage reflects the fragmentary nature of the scroll, not a significantly different Hebrew text that served as the translator’s source text (its Vorlage). In the transliteration of line 5 in 8Ḥev 1 on p. 23, the masculine singular pronoun (autos) is not present in the available fragment, but most assume it would have been present if we had a fuller version of the text. One should also note that 8Ḥev 1 is written in capital letters and does not use breathing marks. This is a physical characteristic of the manuscript, but it has no effect on the meaning. I have chosen not to capitalize the transliteration for purely esthetic reasons.

38. The ancient manuscript evidence containing portions of verses from the book of Micah appears in four scrolls: 4Q81: Mic 5:2–3(1–2); 4Q82: Mic 1:7, 12–15; 2:3–4; 3:12; 4:1–2; 5:7–8(6–7); 7:2–3, 20; 8Ḥev 1: Mic 1:1–8; 2:7–8; 3:5–6; 4:3–10; 5:2–7(1–6); Mur 88: Mic 1:1–5:2, 6–15; 6:1–7, 11–16; 7:1–20. All four of these scrolls contain texts from other books in the Twelve. See the complete list of texts in English translation on the web: http://dssenglishbible.com/ScrollsMinorProphets.htm.

39. Some Hebrew manuscripts found in Qumran do the same thing (e.g., 1Q14). See Ego et al., Minor Prophets, 90.

40. Regarding scribal competence, see Carr, Writing on the Tablet of the Heart, especially his discussions of scribal education on 8–14, 169–73; and van der Toorn, Scribal Culture and the Making of the Hebrew Bible, especially his ruminations regarding the Hebrew Bible as a product of the scribal workshop in the temple.

41. See the work of Molly M. Zahn, Genres of Rewriting in Second Temple Judaism: Scribal Composition and Transmission (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2020).

42. See the more extensive introduction to the Book of the Twelve in Nogalski, Joel, Obadiah, and Jonah, 1–12. This scroll is also called the Minor Prophets (stressing the size of the twelve writings), the Twelve (emphasizing that the parts have some sort of coherence as a collection), or the Twelve Prophets (emphasizing the individuality of the individual prophetic writing). That discussion treats the reasons why recent scholarship has taken up an ancient tradition that the twelve prophets (Hosea–Malachi) constitute a canonical unit whose writings were intended to be read together. These writings, according to Jewish and Christian sources appearing between 200 BCE and the eighth century CE, were written on a single scroll and counted as one book (not twelve). In my commentaries, I treat the Twelve as an editorially created scroll that constitutes one of the four scrolls of the Latter Prophets (which include Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the Twelve). I argue on the one hand that the scroll of the Twelve did not arise haphazardly, but, on the other hand, I argue that one should not assume that the original formulation of every text within the Twelve stems from the same milieu. Nevertheless, enough evidence has been put forward to suggest that some texts represent editorial insertions or compositions that invite readers (ancient and modern) to ask how the twelve prophetic writings function as a literary collection. For this reason, the introduction to Micah in this volume offers suggestions for understanding how the book functions within the larger collection (as with the previously published introductions in Nogalski, Joel, Obadiah, and Jonah, 42–58, 219–21, 349–52).

43. The fixed sequence of the Twelve was not always the same. Two sequences predominate: that of the MT and of the Septuagint. English Bibles follow the sequence of the MT. The fact that these writings are counted as a single scroll does not, however, negate the fact that the individual prophetic writings were also treated on their own (such as the Habakuk Pesher found at Qumran) or grouped together for specific reasons (e.g., the three eighth-century prophets of Hosea, Amos, and Micah in the Septuagint order). The twelve writings appear in a different order in the Septuagint, where Hosea, Amos, and Micah appear as the first three writings in the Twelve. They appear in the same order as they do in the MT (Hebrew), and the next three writings (Joel, Obadiah, and Jonah) also appear in the same sequence as they do in the MT. Grouping Hosea, Amos, and Micah at the beginning of the scroll highlights the prophetic activity in the eighth century (since all three have superscriptions that mention eighth-century kings), while Nahum–Malachi follow in the same order as the MT. This rearrangement suggests that the Septuagint order represents a sequence of writings that derive from the MT and not the other way around. See Nogalski, Introduction to the Hebrew Prophets, 98.

44. Haggai and Zech 1–8 also contain dated superscriptions that appear in chronological order and those superscriptions share other stylistic characteristics suggesting that these two books were edited together to document the prophetic role in reconstructing the temple. These superscriptions all date to the second or fourth year of Darius II (520, 518 BCE). See Nogalski, Literary Precursors, 216–82, esp. the summary on 276–82.

45. Jonah, son of Amittai, prophesied in the time of Jeroboam II according to 2 Kgs 14:25, meaning that the book would logically fit between Amos and Micah, since Jeroboam II is mentioned in Amos 1:1, but Mic 1:1 lists Jotham as the earliest of the three kings mentioned in Micah. Jotham ruled Judah after Jeroboam II, king of Israel, died (though part of their reigns overlapped). Nahum deals with the fall of the Assyrian Empire and Nineveh’s defeat, an event that occurred in 612 BCE, and Habakkuk assumes Yahweh’s sending of Babylon to attack Judah and Jerusalem. When paired together, Nahum and Habakkuk largely fill in the gap of time between Micah and Zephaniah. Malachi is placed after Zechariah because the temple has been rebuilt (which has yet to happen in Haggai and Zechariah). Also, the Persian loanword for governor in Mal 1:8 assumes a Persian ruler. Only Joel and Obadiah do not explicitly owe their position to chronology. For a discussion of the location of Joel and Obadiah in the Twelve, see Nogalski, Joel, Obadiah, and Jonah, 9–12.

46. These passages come from different time periods, thus exhibiting a range of attitudes. The latest (Neh 9:32) accepts the destruction of Jerusalem as punishment from Yahweh. Nehemiah 9:32 recounts Ezra’s prayer in the time of Nehemiah, meaning it cannot have been composed prior to the time of Nehemiah’s arrival (445 BCE). The date of 2 Kgs 17 is likely associated with the composition of the Deuteronomistic History in the mid-sixth century. The bulk of Isa 10 may be dated with relative confidence to the earliest collections that joined portions of Isa 1–11, though precisely how early these chapters were joined together is still debated. A number of commentators see Isa 1–11 as an adaptation of the words of judgment against the Northern Kingdom by Amos, the earliest of the eighth-century prophets. Most, however, argue that much of Isa 1–11 came together as a collection relatively early in the seventh century to shape the memory of Isaiah’s activity. Portions of Isa 10 may, however, relate to a so-called Assyria redaction later in the seventh century, closer to the time of Josiah. It should be noted, in this respect, that Isa 10 presupposes the destruction of Samaria in 722 BCE, one of six cities mentioned in 10:9, 11 that the king of Assyria claims to have already destroyed. The fact that Samaria is already destroyed (10:11) and that the king of Assyria intends to move on Jerusalem suggests knowledge of Sennacherib’s siege at the end of the eighth century may already be in view. For more detailed analysis of debates concerning the dating of these texts, see Joseph Blenkinsopp, Isaiah 1–39: A New Translation with Introduction and Commentary, AB 19 (New York: Doubleday, 2000), 252–54; David M. Carr, The Formation of the Hebrew Bible: A New Reconstruction (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2011), 326–27; Konrad Schmid, The Old Testament: A Literary History, trans. Linda M. Maloney (Minneapolis: Fortress, 2012), 115–19, 125, 146; and Nogalski, Introduction to the Hebrew Prophets, 2–12.

47. See the discussion of the “sin(s) of Jeroboam” and Mic 1–3 as a collection above in the section of this introduction titled, “Authorship and Place of Origin.”

48. Jonah’s speech in Jonah 3:4 contains only five words in Hebrew (‘ôd ’arbāʿaîm yôm wənînwēh nehpāket). Translated woodenly, the speech states, “yet-forty-days-and-Nineveh-overthrown.”

49. See James D. Nogalski, “The Book of the Twelve Is Not a Hypothesis,” in The Book of the Twelve—One Book or Many? Metz Conference Proceedings 5–7 November 2015, ed. Elena Di Pede and Donatella Scaiola, FAT 2/91 (Tübingen: Mohr Siebeck, 2016), 37–59. Several interpreters (Sirach, Jerome, Tobit, and Josephus) provide evidence that ancient authors do more than attest to a scroll containing twelve independent writings. Rather, in several ways they manifest various “reading strategies” of the scroll that pick up on recurring thematic, linguistic, and chronological interconnections between and among writings in the Book of the Twelve. Such readings may not have been the only, or even the dominant model, but the presence of these discussions and interpretive moves means that some sense of the whole did find its way into ancient literary works.

50. See further discussions in Walther Zimmerli, “Vom Prophetenwort zum Prophetenbuch,” TLZ 104 (1979): 481–96; and Walter Brueggemann and Tod Lingafelt, An Introduction to the Old Testament: The Canon and Christian Imagination, 3rd ed. (Louisville: Westminster John Knox, 2020), 131–38.

51. See the discussion of the debate from two perspectives in Ehud Ben Zvi, James Nogalski, and Thomas Römer, Two Sides of a Coin: Juxtaposing Views on Interpreting the Book of the Twelve/the Twelve Prophetic Books, Analecta Gorgiana (Piscataway, NJ: Gorgias, 2009), 16–22; Nogalski, “Book of the Twelve Is Not a Hypothesis,” 37–59.

52. For a history of the term and assessment of the various exegetical models used by proponents and opponents of the term, see Nicholas K. Werse, Reconsidering the Book of the Four: The Shaping of Hosea, Amos, Micah, and Zephaniah as an Early Prophetic Collection, BZAW 517 (Berlin: de Gruyter, 2019), 1–29.

53. Note especially the promise or hope for Judah (in Hos 1:7, 11; 4:15; 11:12) that becomes increasingly impossible because positive references to Judah give way to judgment on Judah as well as Israel (Hos 1:1, 7, 11; 4:15; 5:5, 10, 12–14; 6:4, 11; 8:14; 10:11; 11:12; 12:2). Notably, the hope expressed in Hos 1:11 as an interpretation of the promise after the birth of Hosea’s third child, who is given the name Lo-Ammi (which means “not my people”). Hosea 1:11 offers the hope that Judah and Israel will be gathered together and “shall appoint for themselves one head.” This promise, like Amos 9:11, assumes that this leader will descend from David. It is inconceivable that this “one head” would be anyone other than a descendant of David, given that the final shaping of Hosea reflects a location in Judah. See Paul R. Redditt, “The King in Haggai–Zechariah 1–8 and the Book of the Twelve,” in Tradition and Transition: Haggai and Zechariah 1–8 in the Trajectory of Hebrew Theology, ed. Mark J. Boda and Michael Floyd, LHBOTS 475 (London: Τ&Τ Clark, 2008), 56–82.

54. Amos 9:11 reflects a time after Judah is destroyed (post-587 BCE), not Samaria or Bethel. Its reference to “the fallen booth of David” refers to the kingdom of Judah or, more specifically, to Jerusalem. The reference in 9:14 to “my people Israel” should be interpreted in light of the language of restoring a Davidic king “as in the days of old” in 9:11. Assuming that “Israel” here includes the former Northern Kingdom, its remnant will not be a separate kingdom, but a portion of the kingdom as it existed in traditions concerning David and Solomon, before Jeroboam I seceded (with ten of the twelve tribes) after Solomon’s son Rehoboam came to power after Solomon’s death.

55. See the commentary on 4:1 regarding the marginal note left by the Masoretes denoting the verse as the midpoint of the scroll of the Twelve Prophets.

56. Consider Jeremiah, Uriah, and Amos. Jeremiah confronted several kings of Judah. For doing so, he was thrown into the bottom of a cistern and fed only enough to barely survive. He was eventually released, but Uriah, who spoke the same message as Jeremiah (26:20–24), was hunted down and killed on orders from Jehoiakim, king of Judah. In Amos 7:10–17, Amos was confronted by Amaziah, the high priest at Bethel, and told to return to his own home. The priest had informed Jeroboam, king of Israel, that Amos had threatened the destruction of the country and the life of the king (7:10–11). He arrogantly reports this message as though Amos were a traitor, and he refers to the prophet’s speech as the “words of Amos.” In response, Amos immediately begins speaking words of judgment to Amaziah, recounting his calling as a prophet (7:14–15) before commanding Amaziah to “hear the word of Yahweh” that is directed specifically against Amaziah (7:16).

57. E.g., see Mays, 75–76; and the discussion in Smith-Christopher, 104–7.

58. See the chart illustrating the length of words of doom, distress, and hope in Leslie C. Allen, The Books of Joel, Obadiah, Jonah, and Micah, NICOT (Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1976), 260.
